It has been mentioned that the great Northern Railway of Ireland has already paid £150,000 in compensation for the frightful gantsh to a school excursion train on their system, when eighty per- sons were killed and between two and three htn- dred injured. There are more to pay yet, for all the claims are not satisfied.

h. member of the Rouse ot Commons told the following story about Lord liartington in the smoking-room recently. When his lordship was making his maiden speech he yawned in the middle of it. upon which Mr.' Disraeli remarked, "The man who bag the pluck to do that will be Prime Minister of England yet."

When the Local Government Bill was in Commit- tee, Mr. Seale-Hayne moved a resolution in favour of amending the law in regard to the appoint mitt of justices of the peace by the introduction of the electoral principle. Sir William Harcourt in the course of debate expressed his approval of the slug- , gestion, which was, nevertheless, negatived. Mr. Seale-Hayne• has prepared a Bill embodying the principle, and has obtained the first place on the 10th of March for discussion of the second reading.

Messrs. Henry Matthews and Joseph Chanicellain appeared side by side on the Birmingham platform on Tuesday and Mr. Matthews improved Ile occa- sion by likening the alliance of Tory and Chamber- lainite to the union of husband and wife. God bless the happy: pair! It rather spoils the effect of illus- tration, however, that it should have come from Mr. Matthews, who has never been married at all, instead of from our Joseph, who has been married so frequently,

A Vienna Correspondent states that the son of Count Pista: Karolyi, who eloped some time ago with a young (Jewess, a singer in a miall theatre, has written to his mother. from Boston, asking her pardon, telling her he had already manied the girl he loved, and begging her to pay out of the money that would, at some time come to him a debt of 50,000 florins he had incurred. Having no hope ever to reconcile his family to his marriage, he had made hislnind up to become an American citizen and live by his:work.

Sir William Tlarcourt and Mr. Jolam Morley have differed in, opinion, but it is an exaggeration to say that they have quarrelled 'so seriously that Mr. Gladstone had to be called in to compose their differences. There is no actual quarrel. Sir William llarcourt entertains a very much stronger feeling against Parnellism than does Mr. Morley. Mr. Mor- ley would keep open the door of reconciliation ; Sir William would close it. That istke beginning and the end of the " quarrel."

-- Having been informed that grey hair is coming into fashion, I took the opportunity of a represent- ative gathering of society folk the other evening to glance at the coiffure of ladies. Tile merest glance round the assemblage was sufficient to show that the fashion of grey hair is a grisly fact. A charm- ing lady. near me, who did not lob t: a day older than thirty, was quite grey, and within conversational distance there were at least half a dozen ladies with a more or less pronounced turn of grey in their hair. I take it that this fashion it a revolt against the all but universal system of dying the hair to a fashionable colour.

Visitors to Paris may have noticed some time since in the windows of fashionable -stationers rows of sealing-wax of all hues and shadea, and ranged in order like the colours of the spectrum. It appears that a meaning attaches to each of these colours. Thus, white sealing-wax meanse.lproposal of marri- age; black, a death; violet, condolences; invitations to dinner are sealed with chocolate colour; vermil- lion is used for business lettere, ruby colour by fortunate lovers; green means hope; brown, melan- choly (derived possibly from brawn study); blue, constancy; yellow, jealousy; pale -green conveys a reproof; pink is used by young :ladies, and grey between friends.

There is rejoicing among the friends of temper- ance in the fact that they now number an English duchess among their ranks. The new Duchess of Bedford, hitherto the AlarchioneselTavistock, is like her sister, .Lady Henry Somerset, a strict teetotaller. Other lady 'members of the English nobility who have enlisted: in the cause ot temperance are the Countess of Carlisle and the Countess of Ellesmere. Lady Carlisle is, moreover, well known for her active interest in the woman's rights movement and in allmatters relating to the progress of women. She is ever ready to aid genuinely useful movements with her purse as well as her time.

When Sir John Pope Hennessy was first in the House of Commons, he on one occasion seconded the Bill ,:)f an agedinember for preventing persons from standing outside windows while cleaning them. The member, then an old man, had for fifty years been • regularly endeavouring to pass Chis Bill. Ile said to Sir John," You see, I never -really get an opportunity of explaining the princip'te of my Bill or introducing it. I have been quite misunderstood by the House for these fifty years. I introduced it not for the sake of the window cleaners, but for the sake of the people below on whom they.might fall. The idea of the Bill and the danger to be provided against was suggested to me by the fear that a window cleaner might fall on myself."

Mr. Ernest Hanbury Hankin, the young English man of science, who is said to have discovered at Berlin a "cure" for anthrax, is the son of .43he Rev. Daniel nankin, the vicar of St. Jude's. Mildmay- park. Mr. E. H. Hankin had a very brilliant career as a student at St. Bartholomew's Hospital, where his singular aptitude fon miercscopical work and his general brain power made him one of the favourite pupils of Dr. Klein, theccelehrated bacteriologist and quondam rival of Dr. Koch himself. Even in his student days Ernest Nankin was an experimental scientist to the very finger tips, and was something colossal in the indifference with which he used to handle a whole army of bottles full of germs that could have decimated London.

Mrs. Besant gave an extraordinarily eloquent le,d- ,ture on Saturday in the Steinway Hall on "The Problems & Life and Death." She understands, as so,very few good speakers dthe beauty of rhythm in.a sentence; and the force that is gained by the reiteration of some particular•word. She has evi- dently trained herself in the save school of oratory as .ifolizt 'Bright, and has gone to the same source of litarary and poetic inspiration—>the Bible. She did not trouble her auditors about Mahatmas or any theosophical technicalities. The one central belief upon which She laid stress was the eternity of life. "It is.death," she said, "not life that is the hal- lucination." The spirit alone is eternal. "If the brain decay and the body die," he exclaimed, "shall not the spirit .find some new instrument ? " In this Theosophic faith, Mrs. Besant said, was" an inner fount .of serenity," and to those who -had once held it life could never be the same again."

A Correspondent tells a curious story of the late Dr. McVicar, of Moffatt, visiting the Crichton In- stitution, taking with iim Sir James Crichton Browne, then a child of four years old. As they entered the refractory male ward, a man of colossal stature, in a paroxysm of furious mania, came rush- ing from the far end of it towards them. Dr. McVicar involuntarily stepped back towards the door, while the keepers formed a cordon around him. But to his horror, the naext moment it was observed that the boy had let go his hand and slipped between the attendants and Was advancing towards the maniac. A terrible tragedy seemed imminent, but happily when the child, unconscious of danger, held out his hand, the madman stopped abruptly, gazed at himi intently for.a moment, then knelt down, took him n his arms, and fondled him with all a woman's tenderness. It has not been , given to every eminent practitioner to commence his acquaintance with the characteristics of in- sanity either at co tender all @C,'C. -QP tiom go exciting.

As a great deal of nonsense has been talked latterly about Lord Revelstoke's present income, it may ILL once be asserted that absolutely everything he has has been handed over to the trustees. An annual allowance of slightly over £2,000 has been granted to him by the Baring family till the close of the liquidation, and practically this is all left to Mind his former wealth.

Teprd Salisbury frankly admitted at the Catictton Chtb last year that if the Coneervatives dealt with assisted education "they might put the voluntary schools in a position from which no future hostile majority could dislodge them." Their .diAodgement will be a very simple matter. If the 'Tories carry their bastard free education scheme the Liberals will the first time they are in dice bring it to a logical end by putting all schools under popular control. There must be no taxaticu without repre- sentation. Popular control must inevitably follow popular support.

The " World " says :—There have been gay doings at Derby lately. Sir Andrew and Lady Walker gave a brilliant ball at Osmaston Manor in honour of Miss Walker's debut, at which some 300 guests were present; .and Lady Walker's house party in- cluded Lady Carew and Miss Lethbridge, Lord and Lady Harrington, the Hon. Mrs. and Miss Morton, Mrs. and Miss Stanley Clarke. Lord Henry Bentinck, and Mr. Darby Griffiths. A charming ballroom was erected for the occasion, and supper was served in the winter garden. Dancing was kept up with spirit till the small hours. Lady Carew tore a white frock to ribbons, and appeared later looking ! very handsome in red, and her diamonds were very fine. Lady Walker's diamonds were also note- worthy. She were yellow, and Miss Walker, the debutante, of course wore white. Mrs. Court wore a remarkable mixture of red and green, her husband's , colours. Miss Bullock in pink and Mrs. Linton in white both attracted great attention. The Hon. Mrs. Pierpoint looked well in pale blue, L.' lid Lady Parker wore bright red.

(Applause.) eeisee remind...me_ tba,Lin coming along the high road during the morning I had seen an especially Mondayieh canal worker stretched full length on the bank, blissfully oblivious under the combined influence of John Barleycozn and Morpheus, except perhaps in maudlin dreams, of aught that savourod of shovel or pick. As I was standing chatting with my intelligent Scotch acquaintance, he gave a ;sudden whistle, and all his men trooped down from the bridge with an alacrity tbat showed pretty ex- clusively that it was no change of work to which they were called. Iliey made precipitately for a large shed opposite, audit. presently appeared that the whistle wee the signal for dinner, and the shed was really their dining place, half an hour being allowed for the repast. The span of the seeing bridge I may mention is 120 feet, and it, although then in skeleton form, looked as though it would soon assume a finished aspect. Presently I proceeded along the canal bank for, some distance, choosing the direction from which I had come by the main road and walking down the waggon way amidst a perfect congeries of waggons, pumping engines, coal heaps, wooden huts, and debris of various kinds, and keeping my eye on locomotives rushing about hither and thither— apparently in an aimless sort of way-, for they bad no waggotis attached to them. those I saw being all at a standstill. After proceeding about half a mile I CAME TO ACTON GRANGE and there I met with Mr. Joseph Walker, superin- tendent for the Moore section. Ile very courteously and affably supplied me with much much informa- tion that I wanted. The Moore section extends , fromLatchford to Norton, a distance of about five miles —one seventh of the length of the whole canal—and about 1,400 men are employed in it. The section will be spanned by several swing bridges, and one high level road bridge, and there will _be a railway .viaduct at Acton Grange, over which the two lines of tha London and North-Western Railway Company, and the Great .Western Railway Company are to run, the canal com- pany bearing the expense of constructing the viaduct. The opinion is current amongst the people of the locality that there is some doubt as to the Ship Canal Act being carried out in its entirety, and especially as to the making of the Warrington pocks. The Act of Parlia- ment, however, requires that they shall be constructed, and the authorities of Warrington may,' should think,be counted upon to watch their own interest-sin the matter. I returned along the can& by the way I bad come, tak- ing a survey of the bed of it, as I proceeded. The ex- cavation, for the most part, betweeen Acton Grange and Moss• Side, opposite thf village of Moore, has been . ,STOPPED FOR SOME TIME . through the wagon lines laid along the bed of the canal for the conveyance away of the excavated soil, being 'flooded in consequence mainly of the percolation of water from distant springs, through the sandy banks, but partlyalso on accovint of the heavy rains, and the fact that there had lisen a collapse of the pumping ma- chinery, probably through the frost, the repair of the pumps busily proceeding indeed, at the time, at the blacksmiths' shop along the canal side. One great diffi- 'culty in the excavation of this part of the section has been the frequent slipping of the sandy soil from the sides, necessitating the constant packing of them up, and to a certain extent additional digging. Of course these yielding sides will be carefully pitched, otherwise there would be danger of navigation being impeded by the quantity of sand that would be washed down when the canal was full of water. The frost has been a considerable cause of delay, the masons and bricksetters having been compulsorily idle, through it, for about two months, though they resumed work at the latter part of last week. It was a curious sight to see waggons standing in the canal on the rails, end these and the wheels covered with water, a number of cranes and other apparatus also standing partially immersed. But the pumps -vill soon again, let us hope, be in vigorous operation, and this anomalous state of things give place to a scene of a more animated character. lam inclined to think that it will be more than two years before the Moore section of , the canal is completed; though when the canal as a whole will be an _accomplished work I would not like to hazard a guess. This uncertainty did not, how- ever, prevent me as T returned home and passed the wooden huts with which the canal regions are dotted, from picturing colonies of brick houses and factories, taking their places in course of time. The Canal Com- pany have bought and used land for tipping purposes in the Moore as in other sections, and they take due care. to place the sandy soil undermost, doubtless having an eye to the future demand forthe land for manufacturing as well as for agricultural purposes, though whether the soil on some parts will be fit for farm cultivation, is still a problem.

div.head: STORIES OF ANIMALS.
div.p: STORIES OF ANIMALS.

At the monthly meeting of the Kendal Natural history Society, held last night week, Mr. G. W. , Murdoch, editor of the " Westmoreland Gazette," and formerly editor of the" Warrington Guardian" read a paper on "Human reason and animal in- stinct." There waa a large - attenaanoe, aii tiva course of the discussion that ensued, and which went to show the reasoning powers of animals, the following interesting stories wexe told : "A gentleman visiting the zoological collection at Blacktaool, observing that one of the monkeys was troubled with a 'violent cough, offered it a cough lozenge, which was readily accepted and greedily devoured. Two days afterwaras on repeating the visit he was immediately recognised by the monkey. who rushed toward him and held out his hand as if asking for another lozenge." "An organ-grinder, with a monkey, presented himself at the open window oi a room in which a r family had just dined. The good lady of the house ' cut off the loaf, two slices of bread, one of which she buttered and gave to the organ-grinder, handing the other, minus the butter, to the monkey, who, on perceiving that it was dry, threw it back to the donor."

" A settler in Australia had captured, and suc- ceeded in taming, a white cockatoo, a species of bird which frequented the district in immense flocks. At times it was found /necessary to employ boys to frighten these birds from the corn. The tame cockatoo constituted itself into a sort of senti- nel, taking up its position on the roof of the house and giving timely warning of the approach of the raatauders by shouting 'Cockatoos in the corn.' It had also picked up some of the expressions of endear- ment which passed to the husband from his shrew- ish wife, and would apply them to all corners, and the visitor was surprised to hear . himtelf, greeted by some unseen person with the invitation, , Come in, you old fool.'" I A raven kept in confinement had his natural ten- dency to flight kept in check by a long chain which he dropped about the paved yard which formed his prison. On one occasion the chain be- came fixed by one of its links ix the clink between two a the paving stones. Turning round to ascer- tain the nature of the impediment, the raven, after a few seconds' reflection, walked back and lifted the chain out of the chink." •

_ " A sportsman out shooting early in the morn- ing, took with him a blood spaniel, which, in con- sequence of the hoar frost lying thickly on the ground, was unable to use its power of scent. His master, seeing that he had passed close to a furze bush in which a rabbit was concealed, caned the dog and gave him a practical demonstration of his carelessness by kicking the rabbit out of the bush. Shqstly afterwards, in order to show how thoroughly the object lesson had been learned, the dog rushed into a similar-looking bush and presum- ably set a rabbit, which in reality was not there, and when the trick was exposed he showed e de- cided sense of humiliation.

" A Rporteman ferreting along a hedge had left one net insecurely fastened lown, the consequence being that when the rabbit bolted, it carried off the net. The dog, seeing this, rushed after it but only succeeded In catching hold of the peg of the net. Called upon to' hold on,' the dog suddenly stopped, and putting his paw upon the rabbit held it till his waster got hold of it.' 4' A fox terrier, who had acquired the faculty of making a peculiar noise while indulging in a game, was observed to be giving lessons in the art to a companion of the breed, who had evidently in some mysterious-mannerrconveyed to him his desire to be inetruoted.."

div.head: EXPLOSION IN AM-ERICA.
div.p: EXPLOSION IN AM-ERICA.
LOSS OF 110 LIVES.-THE MINE ON 'FIRE

PITTSBURG, WEDNESDAY.—Up to noon 107 bodies have been recovered from the Mammoth Shaft, and it is be- lieved that seventeen more are still in the pit. Only twenty-two of those brought to the surface have been identified, au i the others being mutilated beyond recog- nition.

Fire damp has never heretofore been known to exist in the mine to any appreciable extent. Hundreds of safety gauge lamps which were provided by the com- pany for the use of the miners have consequently never been used, being considered unnecessary. The men were in the habit of.using instead small open-flame lamps, which they wore in their hats.

div.head: HEAR rRENDING SC H NES
div.p: HEAR rRENDING SC H NES

NNW YORK, WEDNESDAY MORNlNG.—Details of the disaster in the Mammoth Pit of the Frick Coke Works, near Mount Pleasant, Pennsylvania, have reached here very slowly. The explosion took place about nine o'clock on Tuesday morning, at a time when a large number of men were below. The news that a catastrophe had occurred spread with the usual terrible rapidity amongst the relatives and friends of the miners', and there was a hurried rusk of fearfal women to the pit's mouth. Nothing could be for some time ascertained with certainty, the interval being a period of awful suspence to the eager crowd on the bhnk. Then it became known that the disaster was due to an explosion of tire damp, and all knew that the loss of life would be great. A long time elapsed before any attempt could be made to explore the workings, owing to the wrecking of the engine house and gear, and to the assumption, subsequently proved to be well-founded, that the atmosphere of the workings would be unfit to breathe. Numbers of men left work in neighbouring pits to hasten to the assistance of their comrades, or if no more could be done, to bring their dead bodies to the bank. Not long after the explosion a fire broke out in the workings, and dense volumes of smoke rolled from the pit's mouth. Fortunately the machinery for working the immense fans was undamaged, and these were Immediately put in operation' and in a short time quenched the flames. By keeping the fans still in action the pit ,was cleared of the obnoxious gases suffi- ciently to enable a rescuing party to descend. There was no lack of volunteers for this work, and the exploration of the workings began. The search was a difficult one, as the plant in the mine includes 509 ovens with their flues and many intricate galleries, several of which had been greatly damaged by the explosion. Some corpses were soon found, and a cage was sent up with a dismal freight. Then others were discovered, and through- out the day no fewer than sixty were raised to the bank. A number of the victimshad died by suffocation after-damp having followed the explosion. Some of the victims were terribly mutilated by the force of the explosion, and the scenes at the pit mouth, as anxious wives and mothers scanned each unrecognisable face, were distressing in the extreme. Of those who escaped death from the explosion nearly all succumbed to the after-damp. Not a soul is left to tell the story of howl the calamity occurred, for the few who were found alive are absolutely without consciousness, and their condi- tion is such that recovery is hopeless. Even now the exact number of deaths is unkn.o,vn, for no accurate re- cord of the men in the pit at the moment of the disaster has been obtainable. The victims, however, number, It is certain' considerably more than 100; the estimates, varying from 110 to 190. Fully sixty of the hapless miners leave widows and families, who will in most cases be destitute. The first explosion is supposed to have been caused by a miner exposing the naked flame of his lamp, •

div.head: VIE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW; OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
div.p: VIE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW; OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVA.NITS COBB, Ja.
CHAPTER XV.

WHAT HAPPENED AT THE DUKE'S BATH. Ruric eye could keep no account of time. Dark- ness, and darkness only, dwelt with him in his prison house—darkness so utter that the only effect of opening the eyes was the nervous reality of the motion. In fact, 'twas lighter with the eyes closed than 'with them opened, for when tightly closed there were peculiar fantastic shapes floating in the imagination, and even this was a relief; and then

thee was it sort of kaleidoscopic succession of colors when the lids were tightly pressed, that seemed grateful to the nerves, and gave variety to the mind. But when the eyes were open only a cola impenetrable blackness was present, within which there were no shapes-no forms—save the one form of utter chaos.

Ruric felt sure he had baen there four days, and at times it appeared longer than that. Food and drink had been brought to him thrice, and he was now without both. His strength had not yet left him, though there were pains in his limbs, and a chilling sensation about the heart. He had broken _

the rope from his arms on the first day of his con- fineMent ; and he had, hoped to overcome the man who brought him food and drink, and thus make his escape; but no human being had yet come in to him. Ills food ha ril been passed in thrGugh a small wicket.
"And this is the end of life !" he murmured to himself as he paced slowly to and fro across the dungeon. "Thus ends all the hopes of youth, and here the prayers of .a lifetime must close in one last

hope—one hope of heaven when eartli—htis-Ta;;;Ja away! My mother, no farewell can reach thee from the lips of thy son. He will lie down in the dark slumber of death, and thou shalt not know his rest- ing-place! And thou, loved one—oh, thou fondly cherished, wildly worshipped being, thy smiles can shine no more for me! Oh, Rosalind, would that I could see thee, but once—that once more I might press thee to my bosom, and bid thee remember me when lam gone. Had I never seen thee I might not be here now! And yet, oh God, for life itself I

would not wipe away the Written story of that holy love from my heart!" The thought of Rosalind came heavily upon him. All else he could give up in a higher hope than that of earth ; hut for her he held a strange fear: She would be another's. "And must it be so?" he continued, after some minutes of painful reflection. " Alas ! she will be nothing to me hereafter! My mother will know her son, bE Rosalind will know another! And yet —she may carry the old love with her always. She may never forget it. Oh, could I but once—" He stopped suddenly, fsr he heard a footfall in the low passage close by the dungeon. He listened, and he heard more. There were several feet—and soon he heard voices. He moved back to the ex- tremity of the vault and listened. The feet. stooped, and the sound of grating iron, like the drawing of a bolt, was heard. Soon afterwards the door was opened, and the light from a lantern flashed-into the place, For a few moments the prisoner was blind by the sudden transition, but by degrees he overcame the difficulty and was able to look up. The first object upon which his eyes fell was the humpbacked priest, Savotano. There were four others behind him, but Ruric noticed them not yet. He saw before him the man whom he believed to be the instrument of his suffering, and with one bound he reached him and felled him to the floor. " Hold ! "cried one of the others—one who held the lantern—" we have come to conduct thee out from here." • "Ha ! Say ye so .? " "Most. surely we have." "Then stand aside and let me go."' "Just as you say. The doors are open, and you may go. You may follow us, or you may go in ad- vance." "Then lead on," returned Ruric, "and I will "As you say." - • Thus speaking the man assistenTe—p-figt to his feet, and led him out from the cell. In a few moments more the others went out also, and Ruric preferred to follow. He heard the priest cursing, but he noticed that one of the others' led him off. The youth stepped forth into the passage, but he did not place the fullest confidence in what he had heard. He reached the foot of the stairs, and the others were nearly up. He started to follow them, and had nearly gained the top, when a quick, lightning-like shadow flitted before him. He would have started back, but 'twas too late. There came a blow up4n his head, and with a dull, crashing sensation, he sank down. He realised that he was turned over, and that a rope was being lashed about his arms. But the prisoner had not been fully stunned. lie returned to consciousness as they lifted him to his feet, and his first impulse was to try and force his bonds asunder, but this he could not do. He gazed up now, and and he found only two men with him, and they wore masks upon their faces. They were stout, powerful men, and their very bearing was murderous, and his heart sank within him. "Come," said -one of them. "You'll go with us. We won't force ye if you'll walk." "But where," asked the youth. you ?" "You'll see when you get there. But there's no time to waste; so come." What could the prisoner do? His hands were firmly bound behind ' him, and his great strength availed not a bit. He knew that he could not resist. ,so lie simply bowed his head in token of submis- sion, and prepared to follow his conductors. But they left him not to follow at will. They took him by either arm, and thus led him away, lie remembered the room into which he had been first conducted on the evening of his capture, but he was not detained there. From here along corridor led off to where a wing of the building had been partly torn away, and they soon came to a large circular apartment, in the centre of which was a deep basin, where, in years gone by, people had been wont to bathe. The walls looked grim and ragged by the feeble rays of the fantern, and the chill wind came moaning through the cracks and crevices in the decaying masonry. "There," spoke one of the guides, .as he set his lantern upon the top of a broken column ; "we will stop here. • The words were spoken in a-sort of hushed, un- merciful tone, and Ruric felt them strike fearfully upon him. He gazed upon the man who had spoken, and he saw thathe.was preparing to throw off his pelisse, which he had thus far worn. As soon as this was off, he moved to where his com- panion stood, and commenced whispering. Could Ruric mistake longer? What reason, but one, could there have been for bringing him to such a place? To the left, where the basin had once emptied itself, there was a dark, deep, cave-like place, at the mouth of which a heap of rubbish had collected. What a place in which to - hide a dead body! So thought Burk. But he was startled from the dark reverie by a darker reality. One of the men had taken a club—a long, heavy bludgeon which the youth had not before seen— and was just balancing it in one hand while he spat upon the other. "You will not murder me here in cold blood! " uttered Runic, starting back. The stout ruffian clutched the club in both hands, but made no verbal answer. " Speak ! For God sake, answer me! " the prisoner exclaimed, starting back another pace. "Do you mean to murder me ? " "Why," answered the man with the club, in a cool, off-htinded manner, "since you are so .ansi MIS to know, I'll tell you—You will die within a minute ! " "And will you take the life of one who never harmed . you? Hold! If money be - your object
"What mean

"Stop," interrupted the villain. "You can't argue us out of it in that way. You've got to die. and the sooner you go the sooner you'll get over it. You won't suffer a bit if you don't go to kicking up a fuss. There, now—if you hadn't bothered me 'twould have been all over by this time." Oh ! what would Runic have given at that moment for the use of one of his arms? But that was beyond paying for. Yet he had his feet. He said nothing more, but he allowed the man to come within a few yards of him, and then he prepared for the only means of defence he had. The huge club was raised, and at that moment Runic saw that the other man also had a club. He knew then that they had been concealed there until now.
" Hark!" uttered the second villain, just as his companion had raised his club. "What noise is that? "
"I suppose they're coming to see if we've finished the job," returned the other; "and, by the saints ! we ought to have done it ere this. But they shall find it done! "
The ponderous club was raised again, and with a

quick, decisive movement the man advanced Runic made a movement of the body as though be would bow his head for a stroke. Every nerve and muscle of his frame was set for the trial, and for the instant his heart stood still. Quick as thought his body bent—his right knee was brought almost to his chin—and then, with all the force he could command he planted his foot in the pit of the assassin's stomach. The effect was electrical. The wretch bent like a broken stick, .and sank down without a single sign of life. The second man uttered an oath and sprang for- ward with uplifted club, but Runic easily dodged the blow, and then, as the thought for the first time flashed upon his mind, he darted to where the lantern stood, and overturned .it. He had noticed an open passage close at hand, which seemed to lead to some sort of a dressing-room, and, guided by his memory alone, for it was now dark as Erebus there,he glided swiftly into it. When he knocked over the lantern he had upset column and all, and just as he reached the passage he heard a heavy fall, and he knew that his enemy had tumbled over the fallen column.. Ile heard the curses, loud and deep, which dropped from the lips of the baffled man as he picked him- self up, and in a moment more he was edified by a conversation between the two, for villain number one had revived, though the tone of his voice plainly indicated that he had a severe pain still lingering with him.

" Michael! Michael !" groaned number one; and as he spoke Rorie could hear him scrambling up on his feet. • Ili, Orel," returned number two. "Have ye dropped him?" "No !" cried Michael, with a curse which we do not choose to transcribe. " He's a perfect devil I" " But where's the lantern ?" "He put it out." "But you ought to have knocked him down, you clown.' "So had you." "Me ? by—he kicked me over." " Well—he dodged by me and kicked over the lantern." "But where is he now?" "lie's gone. Bark! hini. Don't you hear?" "Yes—they've caught somebody." ." And of course it's him. He went that way. Let's go and find—". " He did not finish the sentence, for at that mo- ment a voice came up in thunder tones; and it said : RURIC ! Runic !" "Good God !" gasped villaidnumber one.: "What is that?" "Runic! Runic I" "By the living gods! that is not from any of our men !" uttered the second villian. "Ha! they aye coming this way !" "Runic! Runic!" " Where shall we flee?" cried Michael. "There is but one place," returned Orel. • "Here, in the little drawing-room. Come—let's find it. Oh, curses on that gun-maker's head! If he be not the very devil, then he's a bound partner of hia. Have your found the entrance, Michael? "No. It's near.you somewhere. Can't you—lla In ! in ! " At that moment the glare of a flaming torch flashed through the gloom ot the place, and the villains stood revealed. A dozen stout men, all well armed, appeared in the only passage by which theY could make escape, for to have fled into the draw' ing-room of which they had spoken would avail them nothing. • " Ho, villains ! " shouted Valdimir the monk, raig` ing his flaming torch high above his head with Ills left hand, while in his right he waved a heavg. sword," Where is Rorie Nevel ? " "Here! here! "cried our hero, starting forward into the larger room. "What I Safe ?—alive ?—well ? " uttered V.Ol. dimir. "Aye—my noblest of friends. But, oh, east off this accursed bond from my arms. It eats into ale flesh." The rope was quickly taken off, and then the youth embraced his deliverer. No questions Were, asked there. Only a few sincere thanks were red, and then attention was turned to the tviv villains who yet stood trembling near them. Tha had not attempted an 'escape, for the way blocked up. They were quickly secured, and the' the party turned away from the place ; and as thaY went Rorie gave the monk an account of the Mall" tier in which he had been entrapped, and of the events whicsh had trans.:Fired isae. "Merciful Heavens ! " ejaculated Valdimir, r Ruric closed his account of the manner in which ue had overcome the two men who had thought te murder him. "It was a narrow escape." "But I might not have escaped without yollr coming," the youth said, "for they would surelY_ have found me. With my hands lashed behind re as they were.l could not have escaped." "True—true," returned Valdimir thoughtfully'. "It was a narrow chance. But it is over now. "And how gained you the knowledge of ,313. whereabouts?" asked Rorie. I'll explain it to you when we have time. Bli,t :did I understand you to say that the humpbaCke° priest was there ? " "lle carte to my dungeon with the-rest, and he that I knocked down. Have you not foul him?" "to; we have seen nothing of him. We foli two men in the hall and that was all." The place was searched all through for the priest,' but he could not be found, and when Valdimir W. assured that the arch villain had made his'escapeu° prepared to leave the building. The prieonenr; four of them—were led out first, and taken aWLY by the monk's followers. When Rorie reached the street the stars werall_n/1 out, and the cool, frosty air struck gratefully up' his brow. He turned towards his mysterious cer; panions, and under the grateful impulse of t„ moment he, stopped. Be raised his hands towar_„' heaven—uttered one fervent sentence- of thaar"' giving to God—and then moved on again. nkr (To be continued.)

div.head: MURDER OF A STEPFATHER.
div.p: MURDER OF A STEPFATHER.

A brutal murder was committed on Sunday morel in a back court leading to Drygate, Glasgow. It apPetig that Jchn Wood, aged 46, prepared breakfast for family. His stepson, Thomas Johnson, aged 18, was pleased with the meal provided for him, and told W.l stepfather so. They quarrelled, and decided to fight out in the back yard. While exchanging blows ander, son of John Wood, rushed out and separated tlaelf; but•while he was leading his father away Thomas dred a knife 'and stabbed his stepfather in the breast. WO expired almost immediately. The murderer surrende6 himself to the police.

THE RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WORTLEY.—EarI DELAWARR moved for a copy of the report made to the Board of Trade relative to the railway accident at Wortley on the 24th December last. He said the reports on various. railway accidents in the United Kingdom showed that in many eases accidents occurred in -consequence of the men being overworked. Lord BALFOUR of BIIRLEIGH, in reply said it was true that in the case referred to by the noble lord the inspector did call attention to the hours that some of the servants on the Great Northern Ccnipany had worked, but he exonerated these men from any connection with the ccident, and laid the blame on a signalman who had only

been on duty 71. hours. Lord COLVILLE of CuLnoss said Major Marindin, the Board•of Trade Inspector Who reported on the accident, stated that the person responsible for tha collision was a signalman, and no one else. div.p: IRELAND.

• • LAND LEAGUE MEETING. Mr Clancy, M.P., presiding on Tuesday over a meeting of the National League, stated that Mr. Parnell had placed in the hands of the treasurers a sum of £B,OOO, the balance of the old Land League fund, for the relief of the evicted tenants. THE LEADERSHIP QUESTION.

Mr. Justin—SFC—arthy and Mr. Sexton who returned from Boulogne on Saturday night, were on Monday evening eagerly questioned by members of Parliameut and other friends at the House of Commons as.to the re- sult of their latest interview with Messrs. O'Brien and Dillon. The two delegates, however, altogether decline to be drawn as to the nature or outcome of their mis- sion. They say that for the present their lips are sealed by a pledge of secrecy, but a verbal report as to the pro- gress of the negotiations will shortly be presented in confidence to a private meeting of their Parliamentary colleagues. Meantime it may be authoritatively stated that no final settlement has yet been arrived at. Mr. Wm. O'Brien, writing to a Blackburn correspon- dent, with reference to a statement by Sir Wilfrid Law- son that he was doing all he could to destroy the confi- dence of the English Liberal party, says he hopes that Sir W. Lawson and others will be more reserved in their speculations until they learn what his course of action in Boulogne has been.

div.head: MR. PARNELL AT WATERFORD.
div.p: MR. PARNELL AT WATERFORD.

Mr. Parnell arrived at Waterford on Sunday by special train from Limerick Junction, accompanied by Messrs. Leamy and Harrison, M.P. A spacious platform was erected on the hill of Ballvbricken, whence Mr. Parnell addressed a large meeting. He said their enemies had declared that the cause of Ireland was in danger. He assured them it was never in danger. The recent elec- tion at Hartlepool showed that the people in the North of England believed in a full and complete settlement of the Irish question. If the Liberal party did not settle this question they would never return to power. He feared he kad been too amiable to "the Grand Old Man," but he promised he would not be so amiable to him again.

• MR. PARNELL AT ARKLOW. The" Freeman's Journal" reports a visit of Mr. Par- nell to Arklow on Tuesday, where he was enthusiastically received. He attended a public meeting, at which plans were submitted for the completion of harbour works. He said he was glad to find such an organized body as the Sailors' and Firemen's Union and Arklow Ship- wrights, and trusted that there was in store for the people of Ireland legislative independence, without which any exertions for the amelioration of the condition of the people or for the promotion of Irish industry and pros- perity would be of no avail, Mr. Parnell left for Eng- land on Tuesday evening.

div.head: MR M'CARTHY AT MANCHESTER.
div.p: MR M'CARTHY AT MANCHESTER.

Mr. Justin M`Carthy, M.P., on Wednesday night ad- dressed a meeting of the members of the Manchester Reform Club, at which Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., presided. He said he would not discuss the causes that led to the present crisis, except in meetings of his own country- men. The attitude of Ireland to England remained the same as before. The Irish wanted to attain their own nationality, and were firq; in that resolve. Home Rule would be a blessing to both England and Ireland, and, now that the democracy had votes he was sure it would- be granted. He did not want to underrate the niagni- tude of the trouble that had fallen upon the Irish party; but it need not concern or trouble the English people. It would pass away, or be arranged or adjusted: and while there might still be recriminations among Irish members, he did not believe in the lasting nature of any quarrel that had not its roots in some real and genuine principle. Mr. M'Carthy afterwards addressed a meeting of Irish- men in the St. James's Hall.

div.head: RIGHT OF CRITICISM.
div.p: THE RIGHT OF CRITICISM.

Lord Stormouth Darling gave judgment on Tuesday in the Court of Session, Edinburgh, in the action for £lOO brought by Madame Georgina Burns against the Scottish Leader" as damages for an alleged slander contained in a criticism of her performances with the Carl Rosa Opera Company, His lordship absolved the defender, holding that newspapers and the • public have an equal right to criticise a puulic performance favour- ably or unfavourably, so long as the criticism is not merely atyse or invective.

div.head: ILLNESS OF MRS. O'SIIEA.
div.p: ILLNESS OF MRS. O'SIIEA.

The" Pall Mall Gazette" says :—We learn that Mrs. O'Shea has been seriously ill. The recent report that she had gone over to Paris was untrue. In consequence of her illness and of a medical certificate that she was not in a fit state to bear any strain the order of the court taking away the custody. of the children from her has been allowed to remain m abeyance. The probate suit is expected to come on immediately after the Easter vacation.
AN AVALANCHE OF SNOW.
NINETEEN PERSONS BURIED.

According to a telegram from Messina. an immense avalanche of snow has fallen in the commune of Floresta- It hass*ept away eleven houses, burying nineteen per- sons in the -ruins. Only one woman and a child have been discovered alive.

div.head: FATAL RIOT IN AMERICA,
div.p: FATAL RIOT IN AMERICA,

An extraordinary riot has occurred a mong the three hundred labourers employed at the Silver Late Ice Company. They took possession of the lake and in- augurated a reign of terror, raiding all the drinking saloons and nearly killing an old man who tried to defend his property. In a pitched battle with the Sheriff's force, several were injured on both sides, one man fatally.
FIGHT WITH DERVISHES AT SUAKIM.

Early on Tuesday morning a band of dervishes made a raid at Suakim, carrying off a number of cattle from the very walls of the forts. The Egyptian cavalry pur- sued, and in the course of a smart engagement two troopers were killed. Ultimately the dervishes were defeated and forty of their number made prisoners. The Egyptian cavalrysubsequently occupied Ilandoub.

div.head: EDUCATION PROPOSALS.
div.p: THE EDUCATION PROPOSALS.

At the Centenary Hall, London, on Wednesday, the Committee appointed by the Wesleyan Conference to re- port on the question of elementary education, decided to support the policy of extending Board schools every- where in England, unsectarian teaching of the Bible to be included in the curriculum, and in favour of a na- tional system of schools under public management. Lord Derby, speaking at an educational gathering at Bury, on Wednesday night, touched on the subject of free education; commenting on the difficulty of appor- tioning help between voluntary schools and Board Schools, and deprecating any unnecessary interference with the compromise arrived at in 1870. He likewise failed to perceive why parents, of whom three out of every four were able to pay something, should be re- lieved of all obligation to help in giving instruction to their children.

THE ALLEGED TRADE DISPUTE ON
THE SHIP CANAL
INTERVIEW WITH COUNCILLOR FLOOD.

Last week Mr. John Price, agent for the con- tractors of the Manchester Ship Canal, wrote a letter to the papers calling attention tea slight dis- pute with masons working on a new railway bridge that is being built at Latchford, condemning the conduct of the Operative Masons' Society, and giv- ing considerable prominence to the name of Coun- cillor Flood, the district secretary of the Sbciety. In view of this correspondence one of our reporters called upon Councillor Flood, who it will be seen gives an account of the affair which is in some re- spects very different from that of Mr. Price. In order to place both sides of the matter before our readers we will quote Mr. Price's letter which reads as follows : "In consequence of the late severe and continued frost a great number of persons, including masons and brick- layers, have been thrown out of work; and last week some of our officials commenced assistirs such persons, including masons and bricklayers, by giving them tickets for groceries, provisions, &c., which they were previously unable to provide for their wives and families. After such tickets had been distributed on Thursday, the 15th inst., our foreman of No. 6 section of the Manchester Ship Canal offered certain stonemasons some stone copings to dress (piecework) for the bridges on the London and North - Western Railway deviation at Latchford. Although the masons were entirely without work and means of subsistence, the secretary of the Operative Masons' Society informed the men that if they accepted the terms of our foreman and did the wcrk piecework, they would be breaking the rules of their society, and that they must not do the ' work by the piece but must -do it by the day. A number of the men having received these instruc- tions went away, not even commencing •to work; although, as we understood from them, they were pen- niless and without work. However three of the masons, viz., Amos Nelson, Edward Edwards, and Samuel Tomes, commenced work at midday on Thursday, the 15th inst., and continued working until midday on Saturday, the 17th inst. piecework, and they received £1 each. If the men liad worked as ordered i.e. day work, they would only have received the sum of 12s. 9d. each. Amos Nelsen, Edward Edwards, and Samuel Tomes, who had worked up.to Saturday, the 17th instant, as above mentioned received a notice, a eopy of which you will find below, from the district secretary of the Operative Masons' Society. You will, lam sure, agree with me that it is very difficult to help men who have starving families under these circumstances. I find that the dis- trict secretary, Thomas Flood, is actually a town coun- cillor of the borough of Warrington, and he is also in the employment of the London and North-Western Railway Company, occupying the positios of foreman over the company's stonemasons, besides being the district secre- tary of the Operative Masons' Society. Ido not wish to make any comment about the behaviour of the society under such circumstances, as the letter speaks for itself.
COPY OF NOTICE. Pelican Inn, Buttermarket-street, Warrington, Jan. 19, 1891. Mr. Amos Nelson

Sir and Brother,—l am instructed to inform you that you have violated the general rules of the Operative Masons' Society in this district, and thereby subjected yourself to a fine of £2 10s.- and loss of all previous membership, through working piecework contrary to these well-established rules. The above rules will be en- forced if you, or any other stonemason, should continue to work piecework after receiving this notice.—Signed upon behalf of Operative Masons' Society. THOMAS FLOOD, District Secretary.

div.head: TITE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 31, 1891.
div.p: TITE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 31, 1891.

sub-contractor on the Canal works, as it is a.rule of our society that no suspension of work should take place until the employer has been waited upon. For my own part, I have no official influence or power in the matter, beyond an anxiety to see that things are compromised as far as possible between both parties. I had an interview at two o'clock on the Friday with Mr. Silverton, and that is the first appearance I had made on the Ship Canal, and I went a long way in agreeing with his pro- posals as to finding the men work. I went so far as to say that I could mot see that any harm would have been done if the men had continued to work at all events till the end of the week. I asked Mr. Silverton if there was no way by which at least two days work in the week could be given the men, and he replied that there was not unless they ,took piece work. After I had seen Mr. Silverton I saw the men and explained to them the position of affairs, and told them that the best thing for me to do was to write to headquarters for advice. I wrote to headquarters on the Friday night, and on theSuncray morning I got a re- ply back again that tinder no circumstances were the men to work piece work. In my letter I made the case as favourable as I could for the men, pointing out that the work would be a kind of relief work, but at head- quarters they decided that this might be only the thin end of the wedge, and that, however generous Mr. Sil- verton might be, it would be a dangerous precedent to establish, and one that might act prejudically hereafter. After receiving these official instructions, I wrote that letter which Mr. Price quotes. On the same day that I wrote that letter a letter was written by Mr. Silverton's foreman, instructing me that Mr. Silverton had done away with piece work. My letter was addressed to one of the three men who continued at work, he being a member of our society. I heard nothing more of the matter till Mr. Price's letter appeared in the paper. As you may guess, I was annoyed at the tone of that letter, and I have since seen Mr. Price Mr. Walker being with him at the time. I complained of the way in which my name had been introduced, and Mr. Walker said that Mr. Price would see that justice was done me. Mr. Flood said he had been described (not in Mr. Price's letter but in a Tory print) as a "well- paid secretary" who had unnecessarily interfered to stop the men from working. As to being "well- paid," he said the whole of the emolument he had received during the past quarter was half-a-crown, and he appealed to a brother mason who had just called in upon him, as to whether that sum was at all commensurate to the labour entailed by the office he held, a decided opinion in thenegative being given. And with regard to the alleged " uanecessary interference," the statements he had already made effectually disposed of that. As a matter of fact, although he had been a member of his society for 28 years, during the whole of that time he had never held up his hand for a strike. He was an opponent of strikes, because he believed they could almost always be done without. As a further ex- ample of the moderation that was being shown in the present instance, he mentioned that at the meeting of the Masons' Society, held on Monday evening, they had de- cided not to impose the fine which the men who accepted the piece-work had made themselves liable to, but to simply censure them.

div.head: INTERVIEW WITH MR. FLOOD.
div.p: INTERVIEW WITH MR. FLOOD.

The following is the report of one of our representatives of an interview he bad with Councillor Flood, the dis- trict secretary,of the Masons' Society :—" Calling upon Mr. Flood on Wednesday evening I remarked that 1 sup- posed he would have seen the letter Mr. Price had sent to the papers." "Yes," Mr. Flood replied, "I have seen it, and the letter conveys an entirely wrong impression. The cir- cumstances are these: for some six or seven weeks the men have been idle owing to the frost, but on the 13th of this month they were allowed to resume work as usual duringa break in the weather. They continued at work on the Tuesday and Wednesday, but on Thursday morn- ing they were told that they were not to work any longer by the day as the weather was not fit to con- tinue working, but if they chose they might work piece work. They were told that the stone was not wanted just then, but, as a sort of assistance to them and their families, they might continue working by the piece until the weather changed. The men, being members of the Union, with the exception of two, knew it was cdn- trary to, the rules of the Masons' Society to accept this offer of piece work, and they refused it and remained idle until they acquainted me with the case on the Fri- day morning." , "Then you did not," I interposed, " interfere in the first instance and stop the men from working, as Mr. Price seems to infer you did? The men, in fact, knowing the rules of their society, refused of their own accord to accept the piece-work ?" "That is so. The charge Mr. Price lays against me is that I stopped the men from working, while, as a matter of fact I did not know of the suspension of work until thirty hours after it had taken place. The men came down to me on the Friday morning and. acquainted me with the eircumstance, and I told them I could give them no advice until I had seen Mr. Silverton, who is the

div.head: PUBLIC MEETING
div.p: A PUBLIC MEETING

was held, under the presidency of Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P. The body of the hall was well filled, and on the platform were Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P., Sir Richard Marcus Brooke, Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Rev. Dr. Preston, ' Messrs. James Reynolds, J.P., A. Thomas, J.P., J. Meadowcroft, F. A. Lake, J. W. Lightburn, G. Summer- field, J. J. Speakman, T. Ward, and A. Lightburn. Letters of apology f or non-attendance had been received from Mr. Joseph Verdin, J.P. D.L., Major Hazlehurst, J.P., and Dr. Steele, J.P. The Chairman, who was cordially received, referred to the opening of the club, the uses of which could not be too highly estimated. Although tne premises might be unpretentious, they would, he trusted, only be the nucleus of something which might lead to great results. It was for the adherents of Conservative principles and especially working-men, to join the club in such large numbers that the place would be too small for them and thus compel the executive committee to engage more pre- tentious and spacious premises. (Hear, hear.) As Pre- sident of the club he did not care how soon this consum- mation arrived. (Applause.) Alluding to political affairs the Chairman said the results achieved by the Government ought to be highly appreciatied. (Applause.) Whether they looked at home legislation or foreign diplomacy, they saw the benefit of having at the head of affairs men who were able to administrate the different offices of state with the polish of culture and the care of statesmanship, and they might claim, with confidence that the present Government had equalled if not sin.- passed any Government that had been in office for many years past. (Applause.) Mr. Forwood in the course of a long speech,enumerated the measures passed by the present Government not- withstanding Mr. Gladstone's declaration that Ireland blocked the way; and mentioning naval matters, he said there never was a time in the history of the country when the nation had in comparison with the power of other nation, a stronger fleet, a fleet better manned and better equipped and ready at a moment's notice to take the seat in defence of the Empire. (Applause.) They would have before long a very important measure before the House of Commons, to relieve the parents of children attending elementary schools all over the country from the payment of the fees for those children. (Applause.) Their member, Mr. Brunner, when there not very long ago, spoke in favour of free education, but the free edu- cation he wculd give and the free education the Govern- ment would give were two very different things. The

free education the Government meant to give would not injure or close the voluntary schools of the country. (Applause.) The great religious communities of the country, the Church of England. the Wesleyan Metho- dists, and the Roman Catholics had in times gone by made great sacrifices for the construction of schools, and the whole elementary system of education had depended entirely upon these three great communities. If Mr. Brunner had his way he -would give free education, but he would take care that those schools should not any longer be managed by those who had so well man- aged them in the past, but should be handed over to the ratepayers, and only secular education given in them. When Mr. Brunner came there again let them ask him would he support the continuance of the denominational schools of the country. (Hear, hear.) And now he was going to deal for a few moments with their member Mr. Brunner,and Ireland., and the relation of their member to Ireland. A circular was issued last year soliciting subscriptions to aid Ireland's efforts for national adependence, as an expression of confiden^e in the leaders and in their organisation, and Mr. Brunner subscribed £l,OOO to the fund.. Now, the secretary of that fund was a very able and very clever man, a Mr. John E. Redmond, M.P.—(laughter)—and he would read: them an extract, which he had never seen quotedbefore, ; from' a speech made by that gentleman at Glenbrien, county Wexford, on the sth December, 1886, after the defeat of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill. Mr. Red- mond said—" When Mr. Gladstone was defeated in England last year, and when the Tories came into power, they boasted they could govern Ireland by means of the ordinary law. Mr. Gladstone, on the contrary, told the people of England that they had to chose between coercion on the one side and Home Rule on the other. Home Rule was defeated at the last election in Great Britain, and I say advisably that if, in the face of that defeat, the • Tories had been able to rule Ireland with the ordinary law, the result would have been, in England and Scotland, to throw back our cause, perhaps for a generation, and to give the lie direct to the prophecy of Mr. Gladstone.' Now, then, he went on, " We "—the National League, to which Mr. Brunnet subscribed £1,003 (they might imagine Mr. Brunner and Mr. Redmond speaking now) "We have been able to force the Government to give up the ordinary law and to fall back once more on coercion." They had heard a great deal about what was called coer- cion in Ireland. (Applause.) In a speech published on the 31st December, in a local paper, Mr. Brunner said— "it is our duty to free the great name of England from the shame, stain, and disgrace of maintaining such a system (as coercion). I believe that you, when the time comes again, will declare that you are against coercion, and mean to abolish it it you can. Well, of course, if they could prevent Mr. Brunner giving his £l,OOO to maintain coercion, then at once they would have coercion abolished. (Laughter.) Then Mr. Brunner went on to illustrate coercion. Now, in a second speech, Mr. Brun- ner said " they had to get ridof that abominable system of coercion in Ireland, and when they found a priest of the Church being fined £2O for having laid his hand on a lady's shoulder in a friendly manner, and a member of the Irish constabulary, for committing a trespass, was treated ;in a different manner, it seemed to him to be high time they got rid of the removable magistrates and of their masters." Mr. Brunner wished them to nnderstand that this was an illustration of the action of the coercion law, otherwise an inquiry before resident magistrates without a jury ; but let him (Mr. Forwood) lr thgin that it was proved in court that this priest who was presented as having laid hands on a lady's shoulder had called that lady, -who was the wife of a superintendent or officer of constabulary, one of the foulest names a man could apply to any woman, much less to a married woman. That priest was not tried, as Mr. Brunner told them, before a removable magistrate, but before a bench of ordinary magistrates and a very large bench ; and that bench of magistrates unanimously came to the conclusion that the conduct of i the priest justified them in inflicting the very heavy penalty of £2O. (Applause.) Therefore his representa- tion of the case was at fault, and his endeavour to con- nect the Crimes Court and Coercion Act with this case was to mislead them. Then he compared with this the fine of one penny levied on a policeman for trespass in crossing a garden of a cottage, and presenting a pistol at the inmates of the cottage. He (the speaker) did not suppose the policeman did more than a pennyworth of damage, and a man could only be fined for the dam- age he did. As to the pistol, he defied Mr. Brunner to find one iota, of evidence to prove his alleption. Another point rose out of this, and he was inclined to liken their member to the Pharisee ot Bethesda. Talk- ing of the escapade of Mr. Parnell, Mr. Brunner turned up the whites of his eyes, and said—" We have clean hands in the matter." He went on to say that " for his part he thought that Mr. Gladstone had raised himself in the minds of every right.thinking man and woman in England by writing that celebrated and memorableletter to Mr. John Morley, and if there came an election they would sweep the country." The letter of Mr. Gladstone was right and proper, and such as any honourable or right-minded man would write, but no honourable or tight-minded man would endeavour to make political capital out of that letter. (Applause.) Sir Charles Rus- sell had said that it was not until Mr. Gladstone saw the rising and overwhelming tide of public opinion that he felt bound, in the interest of the party he led, to convey to the leader of the Irish people that his continued leadership would have a chilling effect on the enthu- siasm of many staunch friends. He (Mr. Forwood) would not have mentioned this except to show that Mr. Brunner had endeavoured to extract party political cap- ital out of one of the most abominable things ever placed before the British public, and that it was only right that they should know the cant and hyprocrisy that at pre- sent prevailed in the Radical ranks. (Applause.) If the Government could claim their support upon the mea- sures they had mentioned, they must not forget that the great cause for which they were elected in 1836 was still as much to the front as ever. Let them not be deluded with the idea that Home Rule was dead. It was true that there was nothing at present before the coun- try but the words "Home Rule," but let them not think that because the conduct and character of the Irish Nationalists had lately been exposed they were going to give up the object they had in view ;hut let them in sea- son and out of season, through their clubs and their meetings, and above all, in that division of Cheshire, by the early adoption of a sound Unionist candidate, give range to the strength of the Unionist party, and so lend an encouraging hand to the Unionist Onr.srnment in the promotion of ngeful legislation, file integrity or the em- pire, and prosperity abroad. (Loud applause.) Mr. James Reynolds moved a resolution expressing con- fidence in the Government, congratulated it- upon the auccess of its home and foreign policy, and cordially thanked Mr. Forwood for his address. In the course of his speech he said Northwieh Division was misrepresented, but at the next, election he thought they knew as well as he did somebody who would come and run Mr. Brun- ner so hard that he would be glad to get into a hiding place after the next election. (Applause.) They all knew him very well, as he contested the County Coun- cil Election, and he (Mr. Reynolds) thought that at the end of next election Mr. Brunner would be just as much in a minority as the man who opposed him (the proposed candidate) at the County Council Eleetion. (4- f:dense.) Mr. Hancock seconded the resolution, which was supported by Mr. Ward and carried unanimously. After responding Mr. Forwood proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, to. whom he referred in terms of eulogy. The Rev. Canon Wood seconded the proposition, and said his presence there that night was amply justified by Mr. Forwood's declaration on freeeducation. He had shown that Government intended to take a firm stand in favour of religious education throughout the country. (Applause.) The motion was carried by acclamation, and the Chairman having briefly replied, the meeting concluded by the singing of the National Anthem.

div.head: LETTER FROM MR. PRICE.
div.p: LETTER FROM MR. PRICE.
We afterwards wrote to Mr. Price giving him very briefly. an outline of Mr. Flood's version of the affair, and m response to this Mr. Price writes as follows : •

Manchester Ship Canal Contract, Knntsford Road, Latchford, 30th January, 1891. To the Editor of the Warrington "Examiner." • Sir,—Mr. Flood has been to see me and says that the Masons stopped on the Thursday, but they went to him for his advice on the Friday and that he wrote to the Secretary of the Operative Stone Masons' Society, London, for adv:ce as to what he must do and the ad- vice he roceived, from the Secretary was a letter of which I give you a copy below, and on Monday morning the men received what I call a cruel letter from Mr. Flood. These are the facts of the case and I shall be glad if you will publish them in this form.—Yours truly, JOHN PRICE.
(co). Operative Stone Masons' Society, Executive Offices, 15, Stamford-st., Blackfriars, London; S.E. January 17th, 1891.

Sir and Bro.,—Yours just to hand. In reply I have to I refer you to the latter clause of rule 12, page 35,General Rules, and to inform you that if your local rules prohibit piecework, or it has not been the custom to work piece- work in your district, the three men in question are do- ing decidedly wrong by working. The Sub-contractor may appear to be generous, but it appears to me to be the thin end of the wedge to introduce piecework, which if accepted by the men you will have great difficulty in stopping in the future. I should ad- vise you not to be led into a trap of that kind, but refuse to work piecework under any conditions, as it is in opposition to the General Rules and the principles of our trade Union, and will sure to have a disastrous effect if once introduced in your district.—Yours truly, .W. HANCOCK, G.S. To Mr. F. Flood, Sec., Warrington Lodge.

On Thursday morning a prize fight for £5O took place in a room in Birmingham, between Hippy Homer, the champion professional feather-weight, who has lately re- turned from America, and J. Weston.a pugilist of con- siderable reputation. Only six rounds were fought, and Homer had matters all his own way, his opponent hold- ing out his hand in acknowledgment of defeat. Wes- ton was very badly punished. The fight took place with bare knuckles.
OPENING OF A CONSERVATIVE CLUB AT RUNCORN, ATTACK ON MR. BRUNNER BY MR. A. B. FORWOOD, M.P.

For some time past the formation of a Conserva- tive Club for Runcorn has been projected, but the difficulty of Qbtaining a suitable building, retarded the action of the local leaders of the party. Even- tually terms were made with the Westminster Cocoa Rooms Company to rent that part of their premises formerly occupied by the Young Men's Christian Association, and which will no doubt be found suitable for the purpose intended. One room will be devoted to billiards &c., and another will be used as a reading room, while refreshments will be obtainable at reasonable rates. The club will be managed by a committee of fifteen, of whom Mr. G. Summerfield is chairman, Mr. J. J. Speakman vice-chairman, and Messrs. A. Lightburn and P. Hopwood, seretaries. The president is Mr. John Brundrit, J.P. The ceremony of formally opening the club was performed on Saturday evening by Mr. A. B. Forwood M.P., the Financial Secretary to the Admiralty. A large company assembled in the club to take part in this function and Mr. Brundrit conducted the proceedings. Mr. J. W. Lightbiirn, on behalf of of the Cotnmit- tee, gave Mr. Forwood a cordial welcome to the club, and said if the premises had any drawback, it was their limited extent. But this was only the beginning of better things, and Mr. Forwood would be glad to know that they started free from debt. They had placed the club on a firm basis; and he hoped it might long continue to develope and spread those Conservative principles of Which Mr. Forwood was so able an exponent. (Applause.) Mr. Forwood, in declaring the club open, said one of the best signs of healthy political activity was the foundation of clubs such as that, and he con- gratulated the Conservative and Unionist party in Runcorn upon the opening of their first club. In the great Conservative centre of Liverpool clubs had been found of the greatest benefit in party or- ganisation and in bringing members of the party together in a social an:l friendly way. The em- ployed and the employer could there converse and discuss the question of the day. enabling, one another to convey stronger and clearer views to the electors whose votes might have to be canvassed. (Applause.) In conclusion, he urged each member to take a personal interest in the success and welfare of the club, and then from that very modest beginning, they would develope into a larger and more substantial ' building, and they would before long carry the banner of Conservatism and Unionism to victory ia this division of the great county of Cheshire. (Applause.) On the proposition of Mr. G. Summersfield, seconded by Mr. J. J. Speakman, and supported by Mr. T. Ward (Northwich), a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. For- wood for his presence and address. An adjournment was then made to the Public Hall, where

div.head: WAItRINGTON COUNTY COURT TRANSACTIONS.
div.p: WAItRINGTON COUNTY COURT TRANSACTIONS.

A return just issued gives the business transacted in each circuit of county court judges during twelve months. From this we collect the following relat- ing to Warrington. In this circuit there were 25,373 plaints not exceeding £2O entered for trial, against 26,565 in the preceding year; 190 above £2O and not exceeding £5O, against 205: and 2 above £5O against 3. The total amount for which plaints were entered I was £55,818, against £59,971. Of the above plaints 14 were determined by jury, against 14, and 17,366 without, against 18,543. Of these 9,696 judg- ments were given for the plaintiffs against 9,780; for the plaintiffs by consents 6,908 against 8,196; for the plaintiffs by default, 462 against 259. There were 53 nonsuits against 34, and 261 for the defen- dants against 288. There wete 7,618 judgment sum- monses issued against 8,321; of these 5,413 were heard against 6,084. The warrants of commitment issued numbered 2,889 against 2,155,and 157 debtors were imprisoned against 129. There were 7,181 executions against goods issued against 7,426, and 100 sales made against 138. The judgments obtained by plaintiffs on original hearings amounted to £34,536 against £37,533 exclusive of costs, -02,488 against £2,384 and-fees under schedule A. £9,458 against £9,879 and B £359 against £297. The gross total amount of moneys paid to the credit of suitors was £36,477 against £35,693, and that paid to them .£35,049 against £35,562.

Huxley, PROMISOR HUXLEY'S letters to the ' Booths Scheme. fil andon General BOOTH'S "Times"cheme lave been published in pamphlet form by Messrs. MACMILLAN and Co. The pamphlet, which bears the title of "Social Diseases and Worse Remedies," includes in addi- tion to the letters a preface and an introductory easay,which, originally published in 'lBBB, has been reprinted for the occasion. Full opportunity is therefore given of judging of the force of the objections which have been urged by the eminent naturalist; and we must confess after giving them careful consideration that we are disappointed with them. A good deal is advanced to show that per- fection is not to be found either in General BoOTO or the Salvation Army; but it was not to be ex- pected that the leader of the Agnostics would be an admirer of either the one or the other. It seems to us that Professor HITXLEY has not kept it suffi- ciently in mind that the immediate object of the' scheme is to give a lift to those who are down in the world, and who are anxious to honestlY earn their Own living. Granted that what he calls " Corybantic Christianity" is not a thing W be universally desired, and that " autocratic social- ism " may work mischief if given too much plaY) it still remains to be shown that the Salvation Army would do harm in giving what, we may call, first aid to the distressed. There are hundreds of subscribers to General BOOTH'S social scheme who have no sympathy with the Salvation Army, and would not subscribe a penny in its support. TheY believe that it is good to feed the hungry and clothe the naked, whether or not it ends in their professing a creed, always assuming that help IS given in such a way as will not pauperise, and will not result in encouraging idleness, mendicancy, and intemperance. With the main propositions of Professor Ws-- LEY'S essay we entirely agree, and we have no- thing but admiration for the lucid and luminous way in which they are stated; but we do not see in them, as he does, barriers to the success'of General BOOTHS scheme. It is indeed true that "when the price of labour sinks below a certain point, the worker infallibly falls into that condi:, tion which the French 'emphatically call /a misere but what then? Are we to infer that there is 1347 thing for it but to let people starve? Is there ne such a thing as helping a man out of the Slougll of Despond, and giving him such a lift on the riglo road that he will not fall into it again? Our 00 opinion is that help can be given in the way pre- posed ; and that the experiment is worth making even at some risk of failure. Speaking of technic° training, Professor HUXLEY. says :—" This 15 a ease in which we Wit nt twenty year: not of strong Government, but of cheerfu'i and hopeful blundering, and we may be thanldtP lif we get things straight in that time." But Itechnical training the only thing in which we nig be permitted to blunder cheerfully and hopefullY It is not for us to say a word against experiment° in education; we are anxious that they should be made; but we are not less anxious that experiment° should be made ip seeking a way out of " Darkest England"—even if it should take twentyyears and require twenty millions of mosey. We are warned that "There are OW £36,000,000 of people in our island, and every yes' considerably more than 300,000 are added to of, numbers." Further, that "no fiitidle-faddle it the 'distribution of wealth will deliver soeiot, from the tendency to be destroyed, by tb_,,e reproduction within itself, in its intense' form, of that struggle for existence the limitatll of which is the object of Society." This may we',o be, and yet the situation is not so hopeless as t 133,, terrible statement would imply. It is true W:e are increasing in numbers, but What if it can shown that we are as yet increasing in wealth in greater proportion ? In order to give Profeel HUXLEY the benefit in the computation, We assume that the addition to the population Ire year was 400,000. On the other side we have I°_, fact that the addition to the wealth of the netw; was 200 millions sterling, which means a proviSi° of no less than MO per head for each of the nolv comers.
