Mr. Forwood THE Tories of Runcorn have been at taking .a leaf out of the Liberal Runcorn. book in providing themselves with a political club. The institution was formally opened, on Saturday evening, by Mr. A. B. FOR- wool), Financial Secrerary to the Admiralty, who, having nothing satisfactory to say for the Govern- ment, entered into a long-winded and peddling criticism of Mr. Brunner's speeches. His idea- of personal responsibility may be judged from the fact that he quoted a speech made by Mr. E. Red- mond, a member of the National League, and sought to make Mr. Brunner party to it, because he kad subscribed £l,OOO to the funds of the League. As well make Mr. For wood responsible for Mr. Parnell's escapades because, in 1885, when he was in the midst of his intrigue with Mrs. O'Shea, he was at the same time in alliance with the Tory party. As to making political capital out of Mr. Parnell' a fall, Mr. Forwood might have had the wit if he hadn't the decency to say nothing on the subject, since to make any reference to the matter was to direct attention to the fact that just now it is the sole stock-in-trade of the Tory party. It was a Tory M.P., wasn't it? who suggested that "Kitty "was as much deserving of a statue as Joan of Arc, seeing that she promised to become the salvation of the Unionist Party? We are obliged to Mr. Forwood for one thing, and that is for what he has revealed as to the intention of the Government on the question of Free Education. If he has not en- tirely let the cat out of the bag, he has let us have a glimpse at the animal. Studiously vague as his language was, it conveyed the idea that the little plot that is hatching-has fonts object not the free- ing of education, but the binding of it in the chains of sectarianism. Canon Ward, who spoke at the same meeting, said Mr. Forwood had "shown that the Government intended -to take a firm stand in favour of religious education throughout the coun- try." If this means that the taxes of the nation aretobe used in the endowment of particular sects, it is a scheme which will have to be fought from beginning to end. Let the State mind its own business: it has nothing to do with "taking a firm stand "in matters of this kind. At present not a" peony is paid, with the sanction of the law, for religious teaehing; and we are strongly inclined to think that the nation will not tolerate a policy which is retrograde and reactionary. It is possible of course that the Tories may do mischief in the direction,but it is mischief which can and will be sharply remedied when the Liberals come into Powee.
The House of Commons has not

Mr. Bradlaugh justified. only arrived at the conclusion that Mr. BRADLAUGLI was unjustly treated, in 1850, when it refused to allow him either to affirm or take the oath, but it has—so to Speak—put on sackcloth and ashes by actually deciding to expunge the obnoxious resolution from the journals of the House. Owing to severe illness, the member for Northampton could not be in his place on Tuesday night to move the resolu- tion on the subject of which he had given notice; but it was taken up in his absence by Mr. HUNTER, the member for North Aberdeen. He explained that it was framed on the precedent in Wilkes's case; but 'he was authorised to say that there was no desire to press any particular form of motion, so long as the original resolution against Mr. BRADLAUGH was rescinded. Acting as the mouth- piece of the Government, the Solicitor- General immediately opposed the moti on, on the ground that it would be childish to reverse the deci- sion of the House, and that it would be a mark of ignominy on the Parliament of 1880. Mr. GLADSTONE, true to the course he has always taken in the prolonged and memorable contro- versy, showed that the House had acted with excess of jurisdiction, and had set up a precedent which was most dangerous and mischievous. Sir STAFFORD NORTH/30TE, as a Conservative, was cheered by Conservatives in urging that the Government shOuld accept the resolution, a cir- cumstance which opened the eyes of the Ministry to the fact that they were likely to be defeated in their policy of opposition. So Mr. SMITH took upon himself to make an entire change of front. He would not admit that the House had done wrong; but, with curious inconsisteney,he consented to the raotion beirg passed, on the understanding that it did not go beyond formally expunging the resolu- tion of 1880. Sir W. BARTTELOT appealed to the best feelings of the House in saying he trusted that-there would not be a dissentient voice; and this was the case, the motion being carried with- out a division and amid cheers. Mr. BRADLAUGH IS to be congratulated upon this complete vindica- tion of the course he took in the oath controversy; and it is to be hoped—as he has proved an invalu- able member of the House of Commons—that he Will soon be so far restored to health as to be en- abled to resume his Parliamentary duties. _ [Since the above was put in type, the news alas! has reached us that Mr. Bradlaugh is no more. He sud- cumbed to the illness which laid him prostrate at half- Past six yesterday morning. His death is a loss to Par- liament and a loss to the country, for, since he became a Member of the House of Commons, he has displayed the 'highest qualities both as a politician and as a citizen. J

Several letters received late are held over, including one from Mr. Dignum in reply to Mr. Gandy.

It is satisfactory to hear that the shorthand classes in connection with the Warrington Recrea- tive Evening Schools are making rapid progress. It is the right sort of technical Instruction, for the clerk of the future who cannot seize the winged words as they fly will either have a back seat, or no seat at all.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, had occasion to comment at St. Helens, on Tuesday, on the number of children's lives . lost through their clothes taking fire. There have been three cases at St. Helens within a week ! His suggestion that inexpensive fireguards should be provided ought to be acted upon. Granted that every item of ex- pense needs considering in a working-inan's home, we should like to see the head of a family who has lost a child through burning, who does not wish he had provided a fireguard.

Lord Kinnaird has been putting in a timely word for women. Speaking at a meeting of the Factory Helpers' Union, on Saturday, he said— ." For every shilling contributed towards the amelioration of the social and moral condition of workwomen, a pound was subscribed for the bene- fit of men. £750,000 was given by Government for technical education, but he had not seen any of that sum going towards the technical education of women." This will never do ;it must be seen to. Let us have fair-play, my brothers.

Professor Huxley is a ready hand at word-mak- ing and phrase-making. He first used the word Agnostic which is now common stock; and in his recent letter to the " Times " on General Booth's scheme he described the religion of the Salva- tion Army as " Corybantic Christianity." The Corybantes, it may be explained, were an ancient Grecian sect whose rites were distinguished with wild music, dancing, &c. Thus as an outcome of the music, genuflexions, &c., of die Salvationists, we get Corybantic Christianity.

The railway servants in this part of the country are about to show sympathy with their brethren on strike in Scotland. There is to be a public meetingin the Public Hall, Warrington, on Sunday commencing at 3in the afternoon. Sunday is the only day, of course, on which they can hold such a meeting; and it is to be hoped there will be a good attendance of the public who will let it be seen that they are not unmindful of the public safety, and of the hardship to men who are required to work excessively long hours.

There is no unison amongst the Unionists in what they say just now about Home Rule. Mr. Chamberlain says it is as dead as Queen Anne ; but Mr. A. B. Forwood says it is not dead. Which of the oracles is to be believed? Lord Hartington, favouring the moribund theory, tells us that Home Rule is a lifeless corpse—" as if it were not the rule for a corpse to be lifeless. Well, well, we will venture to prophesy, because we know, that by way of exception, Home Rule will be a very lively corpse at the next election.

The Tories of Accrington haven't "got the men," but they have "got the money," for a ten- days' bazaar, which clowdon Saturday, has realized £5,784 19s. Lord Cranborne made a speech at the closing, and, amongst other things,he spoke of Mr. Gladstone and his friends "riding upon the eight hours question or some other question of small im- portance." Now, that is a bit of downright Tory- ism quite worthy of Lord Salisbury's son. All questions in which working-men take a large interest are necessarily of "small importance" from the Tory lordling's point of view.

The Scotchmen of Warrington had their second annual " Burns " dinner on Monday evening; and it is expected they will "keep it up," for the memory of the author of "The Cotter's Saturday night" is worthy of all honour.' It is a matter of course to say that the " haggis formed one of the dishes; and, as the heathen Sassenach cannot be supposed to be familiar with it, perhaps it will be as well to explain that it is "made of liver, lights, heart, &c., minced with onions and boiled in a sheep's stomach."

Burns calls the "haggis "the "great chieftain o' the puddin-race," and, it is hardly necessary to add, that he must be in prime condition who can do justice to the dish. As the poet has it : But mark the rustic, haggis fed; The trembling earth resounds his tread, • Clap in his walie niece a blade, He'll make it whissle ; And legs, an arms, an heads will sued, Like taps o' thrissle. Ye Powers wha mak mankind your care, And dish them out your bill o' fare, Auld Scotland wants no skinking ware That jaups in buggies; . But, if ye want her grateful pray'r, Gie her a haggis!

Lecturing, on Monday night, on "Australia as I saw it," Lord Carrington referred to the de- velopment of Australian nationalism, but ex- plained that the tendency to nationalism would not impair loyalty to the Crown. Quite so; and why should it not be the same with the tendency to nationalism in Ireland? The Prince of Wales, who presided, said "Though we wished the colonies to be independent and free, we were proud to think that they had not. forgotten from whenceq they came, and that the interests of those great colonies were and entirely agreed with the in- terests of Great Britain." Precisely; and why should it not be the same with Ireland, after she becomes as "independent and free" as she would be under Home Rule?

Despite strikes, rabbits, and locusts, Australia is advancing with rapid strides. From a copy of the Melbourne " Argus" dated Dec. 19th, it appears that labourers in Mildura are earning 40s per week. There is a great demand for servants in Melbourne, and the advertisements show that the average wage for " Generals " is from 15s. to 18s. per week. °Some of our under-paid" slaveys" might do worse than save up" and go to Mel- bourne. They would be sure to find either a place or a husband.

The paper to hand is from Mr. J. J. Lever, an old friend and pressman, who, tired of the " orrid grind" at home, has gone to the other side of the world to cultivate oranges and grapes. He went out in R.M.S.S. Oruba which left Plymouth on the 9th November, and was in the gale with the ill- fated Serpent, which refused proffered help (it is stated), and afterwards went to pieces on the coast of Spain. After the gale, the Oruba had good weather, and an altogether good time, reach- ing Australia on the 19th December.

Like the altogether prudent family man that he is, Mr. Lever bought his lot nearly two years ago, and bad it put under cultivation whilst he was preparing to go out. His location is the irrigation colony of Mildura which, once a wilderness, is blossming as the rose. A Special Correspondent of the " Argus " furnishes a long article on "Mildura lievisited." To read it sets one longing to bid good-bye to the smoke-smitten town mid make for the fresh, sunny, healthful, fertile country. , •

Here is an extract to the point : We walk through the grounds with Mr. Hodges. And first, says he. let me explain to you that not one tree you see round about here was planted befcce October last year. You see here but fourteen months' growth. Fourteen months' growth ! We are amongst the vines now. Fourteen months' growth! Are we dreaming? Let us pause for a moment. Let us look carefully at one of these vines, and we will certainly choose one of the best. It is a good stout bush, notstaked aftei the fashion' of our ordinary Victorian vineyards, but growing from a stalk cut almost close to the ground. It has in all nine shoots; they average two feet six inches in length, and we count on them twenty-one bunches of grapes. There is no mistake whatever about it. We verify the date of the planting. In mid-October, 1889, that particular vine was planted. In November, 1890, it gives promise to yield full twsnty pounds of ripe fruit."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 31, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 31, 1891.

Again : "It is a matter for surprise that there are a fine set of labourers in Mildura, smart, cap- able, steady, rattling along with their work through the-day as if they had heart in it, and whistling cheerily as they curie into tea, knowing that plea- sure and opportunity are ahead of them. Be it re- membered, also, that there is no publichouse or drinking-saloon for their impoverishmentor demor- alisation. The company is strong on this point. You may argue against it in the abstract, if you ill, as an infringement d natural liberty and an attempt at sumptuary legislation. but the fact stands that many a score of men in Mildura now are well-to-do and thriving, small eapitalists, or actual, or pro- spective landholders, who, if publichouses had been permitted would have been down in the dregs of poverty and misery, or humping their swags back through the malice. Liquor, of course, is obtainable in Mildura. There is, indeed, a club for those who desire and are qualified for such accommodation, but no drinking bars. I thought maybe the work- men of the settlement would resent this, and be disposed to ask angrily, "Why should the swells,' have their club while the poor man' is denied his beer ?" But having sounded some half-dozen of them, I began to understand that such notions were altogether wrong. These men one and all said they had no desire to be led into temptation. Remove the prohibition and there would be a dozen drink- ing-bars in Mildura within a momth and "where would we be then?" This is the result of Local Option abroad; and what an argument for Local Option athome ! -

BIINCORI4 BOARD SCHOOLS. On Tuesday evening the students attending the even- ing classes in connection with the above schools were entertained by means of the limelight lantern. Mr. Pritchard, chairman of the Board, announced that the Rev. Canon Wood, who was to have given the lecture that evening, was unable to be present through indis- position; and the descriptive readings would be given by Mr. Moulton. The entertainment was then proceeded with. The large number of views consisted of splendid photos of the chief buildings and statues of Florence, to- gether with a numb(r of pictures of Swiss scenery. A pleasant evening concluded with a number of comic slides. The lantern was successfully manipulated by Mr. Bowyer. The following evening the same entertain- ment was given to the boys and girls attending the day schools. HOT WIWIR HRiTlNG.—Garland sends estimates free, Warrington.—Adet.

many of them as truly heathen as they were to be found in the heathen lands on the face of the earth. In the East end, in the particular district in which Mr. Thomp- son worked, there was a population of 300,000 to 400,000, equal to the population of Birmingham, and 48 per cent., or one in every two died, a pauper. It was a terrible fact. The squalor and filth and wretchedness were sonie- thing awful to contemplate. Although only four years had passed since the establishment of the mission, they had ten ministers set apart for the London Mission, all beimg devoted men; they had 20 lay agents, including such men as Mr. Josiah Nixs, and others, who ought to be known, as they were doing a most successful work. (Applause.) They had ten halls, and six old chapels, all Sorts of evangelistic agencies, to keep young men `from going to the bad. He was sure that it was a work that would oommend itself to all. (Applause.) The Rev. Peter Thompson who was introduced by the Chairman as the " dockers' friend," said it was very cheering to them to find that all members and sections of the Church of Christ were represented on that plat- form, as it was only what they were familiar with in their mission work. (Hear, hear.) He represented a population of about 350,000 of the poorest men, the most degraded, the most vicious, the most hopeless, and the most :cursed in every respect on the face of the ' earth. He might say that his area was within the dis- trict where the Whitechapel murders took place. On the very flags where the blood of the harlots was spilt he and the sisters had stood and preached the gospel to fallen women. In his area they had more chronic desti- tution and debauchery than could be found amongst any community. He spoke of the long hours worked by the people and thelow wages earned, and observed that this sweating system was an abomination, and Ma com- munity professing honour and humanity such things could not be tolerated in connection with our common Christianity, and in some way things must alter. (Ap- plause.) He wanted to do his share in altering it. (Hear, hear.) They had new five centres of work, and in connection with them between 8-and-900 met in class, there were 1100 Sunday scholars ; between 900 and 1,000 women in their mothers' meetings ; and in , connection with the children's meetings they had probably 3,000 who were meeting on the premises of the mission every week in the year. Besides this they had n open air services every week, and they had their classes, their girls' home, boys' club, band of hope, tem- perance society, rescue work, and medical mission. The School Board had done a great deal, and had had an in- fluence on their work ' • and suppose General Booth's scheme should have the highest success, it wourd only touch the fringe of the problem in the East end. There were hundreds and thousands of young men of grand capacities, who would be the glory of England if they were only taken in hand. (Applause.) His heart was yearning with a boundless, irrepressible passion to do something for the lads ; to take hold of those bright intelligent boys, to give them a strong helping hand, so that they might come forward robust; sober, righteous, and happy citizens of the nation, and not a curse. (Applause.) Reference had been made to his be- ing the dockers' friend, and he might sly he was proud of that strike. It was one of the grandest records that ever took place in the course of civilization, in the course of labour, disputes, that would ever :be written. A hundred thousand men for 30 days marched through the richest city of the world, and no child was hurt— I (applause)—no shop was plundered— (renewed applause) —no police were needed,and no military were called out. They behaved themaelyes, azd they had a splendid re- cord of the manly behaviour sustained through a very long crisis. (Applause.) He had been asked how to ac- count for it. He observed that over 1,000 men were pro- vided every morning by the mission with breakfast. Soup I and bread were given to over 2,500 women and children every afternoon, and they were instructed in Christian principles. It was not the good employers, but the bad ones, who were the cause of strikes. the dockers felt that their curse was drink, and they asked them again! and again that the Mission would help them to 7, et clear ! of the drink shops. There was a drink shop every 39th I house in the neighbourhood. It was not the fault of the dockers they were there: let them put the blame on the right shoulders. It was done by these in power, but they would claim their right to protect their homes and their children. Why should Duke So-and-so and Earl So-and-so, or Mr. So-and-so, the, millionaire, have the right to say they would have no public-houses on their estate and yet 50,000 working-men have no right to say they would not have a public-house on theirs. (Applause.) They had aslarge interests at stake as the highest noble- man in the land, and they claimed that this scourge should be taken from them. (Applati.e.) It was announced that the collection amounted to £l4O, a declaration which was received with loud applause. . The Rev. W. D. Walters, on behalf of the mission, thanked the Superintendent and his colleagues for having ' so kindly received them into the circuit= They had a friend of the forward movement in Mr. Burson, and they anticipated as a result of that visit much spiritual bene- fit would come to the Runcorn Methodist Church. He thanked all who had taken part in the service and especi- ally Mr. F. J. Norman who had done splendid service fur them. They should regard him as a true friend of the London Mission. (Applause.) He also thanked the - Chairman for his sympathy and appreciation. He made a noble gift and promised a noble subscription. Mr. Speakman moved and Mr. Preston seconded a vote of thanks to the Chairman which was carried, and the meeting was brought to a close. Hymns were sung in the course of the evening, Mr. Grice presiding at the organ.

A WATER SCHEME FOR.FRODSI3AII.

According to instructions the executors of Mr. E. Tim- mins, engineer of Runcorn, submitted, for the considera- tion of the Frodsham Parochial Committee, a scheme for carrying out works of water supply, and with the know- ledge of the district and taking the number of inhabi- tants at 3,000 they had made ample provision for the future. Of the two sites they mentioned Messrs. Tim- mins considered the best one situated behind Main-st., off the Gas Works; and suggested the adoption of this site. They had confined themselves to the distribution of Water at a level not exceeding 18 fet above beach mark on wall near Overton Vicarage „oat*. Any supply beyond this could be made by special.artangement but they could not advise the Committee to extend or increase the working pressure from the present pumping arrangements laid down. The contour line of Frodsham and Overton being so extreme, required full considera- tion. This difficulty they overcame by having one high level covered reservoir of 125,000 gallons capacity, oppo- site the bend of the road near Five Crosses. The six inch

! main to this would apply for pumping and distribution and would be minus any cimplkations of stop valve or double mains, which two reservoirs would give. To obviate the high working pressure this would give at the lower or west end of Frodsham (about nibs. to square inch). We propose a water valve fixed near Main- street crossing, in a suitable building, where Pressure could be regulated at will, and taking the east end, the minimum pressure at ,Mr. Nickson's residence, the "Rock " would be about 30Ibs. per square foot, suffi- cient for domestic use and fire purposes. The well and pumping station they .projsosed to place behind Main- street, at a distance safe from contamination by the Gas Company's gasholder tank. Here they suggested a shallow well, six feet diameter, and 20 feet deep, having a set of three throw pumps worked off a Crossley's Otto Gas Engine, capable of discharging 5,000 gallons per hour into reservoir. A bore hole of Of inches diameter down to 300 feet to be made from surface, and connected to suction-pipe of 'pumps if found necessary ; provision to be Made in enginehouses for duplicate engine and pumps. The sizes and limits of the mains were given. and Mr. Timmins concluded by saying it would be necessary to fix standpipes and tire hydrants, at mot convenient places, which afterwards could be decided upon.—ln the letter accompanying this scheme, Mr. Walter Timmins said the firm estimated the approxi- mate cost of this scheme at £3,000, exclusive of land, Waylearta, easements, and compensation, and service pipes into dwelling houses. They will also undertake to make a 13i chisel boring to 150 feet on the proposed site, to confirm their opinion, for the sum of £75, and,if found necessary,to 'e his s) beyond t depth,los. .' per foot extra to the specified depth of 300 feet, which borehole could afterwards be utilized for the benefit of the works. After a long discussion, the committtee unanimously resolved that the scheme be recommended LA the Central Authority, subject to several alterations in detail. It was also recommended that the authority instrucetheir clerk to communicate with Mr. Higson and the representatives of the late Mrs. Perryn as to whether they would sell or lease to the authority portions of fields shown on the plan and that if they refuse to sell or lease them he ascertain if any of the adjoining lands could be obtained.—Mr. Thomas moved and Mr. Aaron seconded the adoption of the minutes.—ln answer to Mr. Brandreth, the clerk said the cost of the scheme would be a Frodsham charge, and not upon the lordship.—Mr. Brandreth said the committee had spent £1,300 in obtain- ing water at Newton, and he understood that there could be plenty of water obtained if a pump were used.—The Clerk said the Local Government would not sanction that scheme : they said there was not sufficient water.—Mr. Brandreth said if they took water from the Marsh on to the top of the hill, he would guarantee it cost £6,000.— The thairman : .Why should it be so, when the engineers , place it at £3,000 ?—Mr. Brandied' : Then there is the buying of land, wayleaves, and all that.—Mr. Thomas said the estimate for the Newton scheme was something about £B,OOO. This was a cheaper scheme. There was only one wayleave to be got for a Short distance and a piece of land would be required for the reservoir and for the well.—The minutes were approved_

REALM OF THE DISTRICT. The Medical Officer (Dr. Adams) reported two cases of diptheria at a cottage at Sutton. Be noticed a peculiar smell and ascertained that cows were kept in an adjoin- ing building, with only brick wall division. There was nothing else to account for the disease. Typhoid fever had occurred at Alvanley and Overton, the case at the latter place having arisen through the water supply. A case.of puerperal fever had occurred at Five Crosses,

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

The murder is out. Mr. Brunner is not to have the walk-over at the next election, that has been- more than once predicted. Mr. James Reynolds, no doubt, in the exuberance of his joy, let the cat out of the bag on Saturday night, at the Conservative meeting held to celebrate the opening of the new club. We hope he will not get into hot water for his premature declaration, which will put those dreadful Radicals on the alert instead of permitting them to slumber in a state of false security to nearer the day of action.

Although Mr. Reynolds's language is slightly mixed, the meaning is plain, and he who runs may read. Mr. Joseph Verdin havitg rigorously resiSted the blandishmetts of the "great Unionist party," declined to encounter almost certain defeat. The party managers have now come to Runcorn to find a man who will make Mr.Brunner be glad to "keep in a hiding place atter the next election," because Mr. Brunner will be as much in a minority as this doughty gentleman's opponent was at the County Council election.

There is only one personto whom this can refer, and that is our tcwnsman Major Hazlehurst. Bear- ing an honoured name, Major Hazlehurst will al- ways command the respect of the people of Run- corn, but men do not sink their political opinions to do homage to any man or name, and as he fought the County Council election as a non-pnlitical can- didate, that is no guide as to the result of a fight on strict party lines. If he has consented, as Mr. Rey- nolds indicated, to enter the strife of Parliamentary life, he has undertaken a task which he does not ac- urately estimate, and which is doomed to almost a certain failure, in attempting to oust Mr. Brunner L from the representation of Northwich division. One of the finest ineetings ever held in St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel at Runcorn, was that which took place on Wednesday evening in aid of the London Mission. To those on the platform the sight of that noble building crowded in every part was an inspir- ing sight, and from first to last the speakers main- tained a high and lofty idea of the work in progress, and frequently roused the audience to an advanced state of enthusiasm which was reflected in the magnificent collection of .£l4O. One lady was so overcome with the need for grappling with the squalor, filth, and vice, which the missionaries de- picted that she dropped her gold ring into the box as an offering, a circumstance of very rare occurence 1 in our churches and chapels. Any one long resident in Runcorn is acquainted with the ephemeral character of the musical societies ' which have from time to time been established in Runcorn, and it is pleasing to ilnd the Tonic Sol Fa Choir, rejoicing in good seasons and defying bad ones, still carrying on its mission of developing and extending musical culture. There has never been a society in the town which has done so ranch for spreading a thorough knowleage of the " divine art " and one can only grieve that the public does not support the choir in a manner that its labours demand. The second concert of the season will be given on Monday evening next, for which occasion well known and able principals have been engaged, and it is to be hoped that there will he a crowded house to congratulate Mr. J. Holford, G.T.S.C., the conductor of the choir, on his recently earned honours, and to encourage him in the admirable work lie has so assiduously carried on for years past.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN.

In connection with the Oxford University Extension scheme, Mr. H. J. Mac Kinder, M.A., on Friday evening delivered the second of a series of lectures entitled "The growth of the political systems of Europe." The subject dealt with was "Greece," and the lecturer gave an inte- resting account of that ancient empire, elucidating his remarks by means of maps thrown on a screen by the oxy-hydrogen lantern.

Thomas Abrams, flatman of Widnes,' was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Tuesday, charged with neglecting to maintain his six children who are inmates of Runcorn Union Workhouse. Mr. Frodsham, collector to the Union, said the prisoner was sent to gaol fora similar offence twelvemonths ago, and he was now £lO in arrear with his payments. The Guardians had forgiven him about £so.—lnspector Bowyer said the prisoner also owed 355. for the maintenance of a son in the Reformatory. Between the Workhouse and the Reformatory he had all his family kept by the rate- payers.—The 'Bench sentenced the prisoner to two months' hard labour. UMBRELLAS TIE-COVERED at the shortest notice.--.T. & W. Durrox's Sank'-5t., Warrington.—Advt. PROMOTION OF CHRISTIANITY AMONGST THE JEWS. In aid of the Society for promoting Christianity amongst the Jews, a public meeting was held in Trinity schoolroom, on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. P. Spzakinan, C.C. After prayer by the Rev. J. Pomeroy. the Chairman said it gave him great pleasure to be present, and to support a society doing such a good and useful work as the Jews' Society. His aim was to try to be of what service he could in the cause of Christ, and to render what assistance lay in:his power to those who were endeavouring to extend the Gospel. (Applause.) He pointed out what the objects of the society are, and the real and rapid progress it is making in winning the "Lost sheep of the House of Israel." He hoped ere long to be able to see something of that coun- try, so famous in the history of the world—the Holy Land—as it was his intention to accompany Dr. Preston on a visit to Jerusalem very shortly. (Applause.) The Rev. S. Schor then delivered a lecture on the work of the Society, and gave some interesting descriptions of i life and manners n Palestine. The lecture was illus- trated by the magic lantern. On the proposal of Dr. Preston, seconded by Mr. Lea, the usual votes of thanks were accorded. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.-7. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt.
THE BREAD TRADE OF WIDNES.

John Ward, grocer, Ditton, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of sel- ling bread otherwise than by weight. Mr.J. W. Knowles defended, and pleaded not guilty. OR the 22nd inst. P.C. Clark visited the defendant's shop, disguised as a chemical labourer. He purchased a /lb. of cheese and asked fora 21b. loaf, but Mrs. Ward, who was attending to the counter, said they had notie, but they had some loaves they sol at 31d. each, though she did not know what weight they were, He, however, purchased a 41b. loaf, and after Mrs. Ward had wrapped it in a handker- chief, he asked her to weigh it for him, and it was found to be three ounces short. She then weighed another loaf, which was five ounces light. The officer then declared himself, and said he shnuld report the matter.— For the defence, Mr. Knowles contended that the sale was not completed before the loaf was weighed, and that the officer pretended to be drunk, and so alarmed Mrs. Ward,who was in an interestieg condition, that she was unable to attend court that•day. The de- fendant was not aware that bread ought to be weighed, and in his (Mr. Knowles's) opinion three-fourths of the grocers did not know that such was the law. He asked why did 'not the police go to the dealer who sold thousands of loaves in a week, and not make a catch of a man who only sold four dozen. The defendant purchased the loaves from s. wholesale man as teue weight. Competition was so k.e,en in the bread trade in Widnes that, after the bakers' wages; were paid, there was no profit left for the grocer. —The Bench did not think there was much intention to defraud ; but the bread ought to have been weighed be- fore it was sold, and a no of ss. and costs was im- posed.

SHAKESPEARE THEATRE, LIVERPOOL. The pantomime at this place of amusement loses none of its hold on the public mind, and goes with a raciness which has characterised it from the open- ing night. If anything it becomes more lively as the local hits are carried on up to date. The Hon. Mrs. Dunscombe, gains in favour with the audience, her acting and singing being brisk and full of verve. The horizontal bar performances in the seconfl act of the harlequinade are a treat in themselves, the tricks being of a really wonderful nature,and visitors to Liverpool can be sure of a treat at the Shakes- p3are. div.head: SINGULAR FATAL ACCIDENT AT HATTON.
div.p: SINGULAR FATAL ACCIDENT AT HATTON.

Mr. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest at Hatton Arms, Hatton, on Monday on the body of an ofd man named James Burrows, who met with his death under somewhat singular circumstances.—Thotnas Humphreys, joiner, Hatton, said he lived at the house of a daughter of the deceased, who was 81 years of age. He last saw the deceased on Thursday evening at 7.50. He wished to go to bed, but be was told that "it was too early." The deceased then left the house,bUt as he did not return search was made for him. Witness could riot say why deceased went to the place where he was found but the <old man was in his dotage.—Elizabeth Bur- rows, granddaughter of the deceased, having given evidence, P.C. Shatwell deposed to finding the body of the deceased in a ditch near the Hurst Farm abolt half-a-mile from Burrows's house. The body was fully dressed, and deceised's right foot was held fast, under a root. The old man could not have got up, and witness had to saw off the root before he could liberate him. There were no marks of violence on the body.—The jury returned a verdict of "Death from exposure through being entangled by the root of a tree in a wet ditch at Appleton." niumBRELLAs RE-COTERED At the shortest notice.—J. & W Burros's Sankey-t., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: SKATING MATCHES.
div.p: SKATING MATCHES.

An immense crowd of people assembled on Eccles- ton Mere on Sunday afternoon, when a skating I match took place between John Highcock, of Parr, the local 300-yards champion, and Hazeltine, who ,:ts better known as " Donkey " a Abram. The stakes were £l5 aside, and the distance. one mile Mr. James Marsh, of,the Sefton Hotel, was the referee. An easy start was effected, and it was at once evident that Highcock had his man well in hand. He fell twice but was quickly upon his feet each time, and putting in a fine sprint, *on easily by about thirty yards. The time opcupied was three minutes and thirty-three seconds. On Satur- day afternoon, a match took place on Carr Mill Dam, between Jack Not of Billinge and James South- worth, of Hindley. The stakes were X.,15 aside and the distance 300 yards. Pigot got a start but South- worth won easily by ten yards. A match was arranged to take place at Sefton Meadows, Liver- pool, on Monday afternoon, between Highcock and Southworth, the distance to be 30 yards and the stakes £5O aside, the match to come off on Sefton Meadows. Thither a party repaired from St. Helens, but on arriving at the scene of action it was at once apparent that there was no probability of a match. as it was raining heavily, and the ice on the Meadows Lad almost entirely disappeared. The visitors, of course, had no option but to retire much disappointed with the fruitlOss journey. SOU-WESTER ROOF PLATES.—LS. Garland, Builders' Iron- monger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—ildct.
VISIT OF THE LONDON MISSION TO
RUNCORN. MEETING IN ST. PAUL'S CHAPEL

No event has occurred amongst local Wesleyans for many years, which caused such deep and wide- spread interest as the visit of the London Mission last week end. The pulpit of St Paul's Chapel was occupied on Sunday by the Rev. W. D. Walters,secre- tary to the mission,and at both the morning and even- ing service he preached to a large congregation. A , further service was held on Monday afternoon, and the announcement that the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes:, the celebrated chief of the %Vest End Mission was to -preach, drew together a congregation of large pro- portions, but Mr. Hughes was unable to fulfil his engagement, and hisiplace was taken by the Rev, Peter Thompson, of the East End Mission, who delivered an eloquent discourse. In the evening a public meeting was held,and the spacious sacred edifice was crowded in every part, seats having to be provided in the aisles. Mr. C. E. Parker of,Penketh, presided and he was supported byl the deputation from the mission,the Rev. W. D. Walters, , Rev. Peter Thompson, Sister Jo'sephine and Mr. Josiah Nix. There were also on the platform the Revs. H. Burson, W. Kendrew, J. Judson Dr. Preston (Church of England), C. Finch (Primitive), J. Simpson (Congrega- tional), J. Martin (Methodist Free Church), T. Law (Widnes), and P. Pingev (Frodiliain) ; M‘ssrs. P. Speak- man C.C., S. Taylor, J. Simpson,T. Handley, S. Pope, F. J. Norman, R. H. Posnett, G. Bellamy, J. Unsworth, and T. Simister. The Chairman, in opening the, proceedings, said the London Mission was founded on the principles laid down by our Saviour, when he said to his followers "Give ye them to eat." There were in the metropolis tens of thou- sands who wer..hungry for bread- and also for love, for light, and for faith; and they rejoiced that good men and true had dedicated their lives and their services to that great and good work, and they said " God bless the London Mission." (Applause) Mr. Josiah Nixs, said he was as disappointed as the audience could be at the absence of Mr. Hughes, whose place he had been disputed to take. He described the great-success which had attended the West End Mission since it was started three years ago, and dealing with ' his own special work at Wardour Hall said he had in conducting his mission learned some very valuable lessons from the public-houses in grappling with the sin and poverty and lust of the city. People live in single rooms for which they had to pay as much as Bs. per week, and the owners looked better after their hunters and their swine than they looked after their tenants. Money was wrung out of poor widows in order to keep these Hell men in luxury and wealth. At Wardour Hall they fed 5,000 a week with good soup,and ,some of the people got ccnverted. In eleven Weeks 92 women and 37 men had passed through the inquiry rooms and they had 4aken 546 pledges since the first Week in December. (Applause.) On the last night in the old year they gave a dinner for drunkards, and of the 300 who came 100 signed the pledge. (Applause.) In their mission they fed the hungry,clotheci the naked, and preached the Gospel. It was a life of joy and not of sacrifice for the benefit of mankind and the glory of God. (Applause.) Sister Josephine (one of the sisters of the people), said the work of the sisters was to try and help those who had sunk so low in sin that they felt lost for ever. They went amongst the very lowest and never feared to go into ' their houses to try to relieve them. (Applause) She described in touching fashion the various works of the sisters and the agencies they had for dealing with chil- dren, young girls, and women, a,ud pourtrayed in grap- hic fashion the dreadful misery and want they encoun- tered. Drink, she said, was the one thing that prevented them having greater results with their work. It was through drink every other sin was committed and the immorality inthe district where she worked was fearful. She asked for the prayers of those present to enable her/ and her sisters to pursue their labours with. greater suc- cess. (Applause.) The Rev. W. D. Walters said there were no fewer than .50 Sisters of the People engaged in that self-sacrificing work, and he assured them that all the workers in the mission had an intense desire to make the people Christian and strove to do their work in an unsectarian spirit. That was one point they kept steadily before them. (Applause.) It was only a few years ago that the London Mission was started, and they were indebted to their Congregational friends for the inspiration. It was found that there was an immense number of people in the Metropolis who never entered any sanctuary,

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIA.NS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIA.NS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar— dians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon. There were present Major J. W. Wareing (chairman), Rev. S. A.K. Sylvester, Rev. Dean: Finegan, Messrs. W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, W. Middle- hunt, J. Ranson, J. Ellison, James Burchall, W. Daine, E. Syder, J. Davies, J. Peover, E. Birchall, J. Mercer, W. Borrows, J. Griffiths, W.Twist,Joseph Birchall, W.Lowe, H. Fulme, J. Marsh, P. Longton, J.Kenwright, and S.H. Hartley (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported, that there were 603 inmates this week,6l7 last weekand 607 in the corresponding week last year; 65 vagrants had been re- lieved against 42 last year.

INcitiisma REMUNERATION.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that they had had under consideration the application made by Messrs. J. Kitchen and H. A. Twist, assistant overseers for Sutton and St. Helens districts respectively, for additional rem- uneration, and directed the Guardians to pay to them such additional sums as would make their remuneration for the year ending 25th March £l6O each. THE WOOLTON SCHOOL ATTENDANCH OFFICER.—The Local Government Board wrote approving the re-ap- pointment of Mr. R. G. Waterman as school attendance officer and inquiry officer for the Woolton district at a salary of £BO per annum. _

TiE BOARD AND =COUNTY BATE.—The Clerk read a letter from the Clerk to the Lancashire County Council with respect to the proposed new basis of valuation for county rating purposes. In suggesting that the com- munication should be referred to the Assessment Com- mittee the Clerk stated that they had the same matter before them seven or eight years ago, and the Guardians were then fortunate in obtaining a reduction of some- thing like £23,000. He thought it would be an advan- tage if the Union was represented when the matter was again brought forward at Preston.—Mr. Middlehurst asked if the proposed changes would be to the disadvan- tage of the Union.—The Clerk replied that it would be a disadvantage if the system was adopted.—lt was then decided that the letter should be referred to the Assess- ment Committee.

TiE AUDIT.—The Clerk reported that since the last meeting the district auditor had attended and gone through the accounts of the Guardians. He was happy to report that there had been no surcharges. (Applause.) TIM GUARDIANS AND THE COUNTY COITNCIL.—The Clerk reported that since the last meeting they had been asked to make their claim upon the County Council showing the amount to which they were entitled under the Local Government Act of 1888. From the County Council they claimed £4OlB is. 7d., and from the St. Helens. County Borough £2650 16.5. 5d., making a total of £6668 18s.

APPOINTMENT OF RELIEVING OFFICERS.—The Board afterwards proceed to elect two relieving officers for the rearranged Widnes relief districts, and Mr. Tyer and Mr. Dame complained that at a special meetingof the Board, a resolution was passed that applications from persons residing outside the Union limits should be excluded. The Chairman said the resolution was passed by a majority of the Board, and discussion on the subject was out of order. Messrs. T. W. Cook (89, Cooper-st., St. Helens, clerk), T. Grant (31, Joseph-st., Widnes, pensioner), IL Hampson (55, Kent-st., IVidnes, time- keeper), J. Middlehurst (foreman St. Helens goods station), G. Oakes (125, Duke-st. St. Helens, clerk), W. iVinstanley (6, Junction-lane, Sutton, assistant school- master), Thomas Roberts (Widnes, assurance agent), and Alfred Wood (22, Deacon-road, Widnes, gas sales- man), appeared before the Board; and ultimately Messrs. Hampson and Wood were appointed to the Wid- nes and Ditton districts respectively, subject to the sanction of the Local Government Board. This was all the business.
RUMOURED LOSS OF A TRANSPORT
AND 700 LIVES

Anxiety is felt at Toulon regarding the French trans- port, Annamite, which is supposed to have foundered with 700 souls aboard, bound for Tonkin. Another telegram from Toulon says :—Great anxiety is felt here in regard to the fate of the French transport l'Annamite, Captain Lemoine, which left Toulon on the first of January with 711 passengers, civil and military, for Cochin China and Tonkin. Rumours are current in naval circles that the Annamite, after embarking a detachment of infantry at Oran, foundered at sea.

Flames broke out on Thursday morning on the premises of a baker named Schornshem, in Hammersmith-road, London, and spread to the foundry of Mr. M. Chamber- lain adjoining. Both places are destroyed, and Minnie Chamberlain, aged 13, was burned to death.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF DR. MANGAN OF RUNCORN".
div.p: MARRIAGE OF DR. MANGAN OF RUNCORN".

Mr. B. Mangan, M.D., of Church-Place, Runcorn, was married on Saturday last to Miss Delia O'Brien daughter of Mr. Austin O'Brien, of Atlantic View, Lisdoonvarna, County Clare, Ireland. The cere- mony took place at the Church of our Lady of Re- fuge, Rathmines, Dublin, in the presence of a num- ber of relatives and friends. The bride, who was attired in a grey travelling costume, was attended by her sister, who was also dressed in grey ; and Dr.. McCambriclge, of Widnes, officiated as best man. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. Michael O'Brien. The offi- ciating clergyman was the Rev. Father Dowley, Adm. of St. ratrick'sChurcb, Waterford, and he was assisted by the Rev. J. P. O'Leary, C.C., Wexford. The guests in- cluded Miss Mangan, Mr. Joseph Mangan (solicitor, Dublin), Dr. Mangan (Dublin), Dr. and Mrs. Heynes (County Clare). After the ceremony the party sat down to breakfast, and later in the day Dr. and Mrs. Mangan left for Bray, thence proceeded to London. The presents were numerous and costly.
CO-OPERATIVE TEA-PARTY AND BALL.

The annual tea party, entertainment, and ball, in connection with Runcorn and Widnes Co-operative Society, took place in Runcorn Public Hall, on Wednesday, and, as usual, was an unqualified suc- cess. About 700 persons were present at tea, and there had to be two "sittings." The ladies who presided over the tables and otherwise assisted were Mesdames Rushton, Fitton, Sillitoe, Ains- worth, J. Shaw, Ellison, Rogerson, Joyce, Leath- wood, Betney, Joseph Stubbs, R. Evans, Bowyer, Ellison, Pendlebury,Cox, T.Price, and Nixon; Misses Rushton, Hassey, Hiudley, Joyce, Royle, Riley, I Worthington, dwards, Wilson, and others. The arrangements had been ably made by a committee consisting of Messrs. T. Ailey (chairman), R. Royle, Worthington, Heatherington, Rogerson, Cropper, Betney, and Watson, and no difficulty was expe- rienced in accommodating and providing for the large number of guests at tea. When the tables had been cleared away, an entertainment was given un- der the presidency of Mr. T. Riley. Mr. greenwood, of Manchester, had been advertised to give an en- tertainment,but he was unable td be present,though a capital substitute was found in Mr. Antonio, of ' Manchester, who greatly amused the audience by his character sketches. Mr. Powell, of lanchester, also gave several recitations in good style. Two cornet solos were contributed by Mr. J. Woods, ac- companied by Mr. Ravenscroft, and he was de- servedly encored for his skilful performance. Sub- sequently dancing was indulged in to the' music of Wood's Quadrille Band, hut the hall was incapable of accommodating all who desired to join in the mazy whirl, and the Co-operative Hall was utilized for the purpose with much advantage.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Colonel Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present: Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. A. Thomas J.P. (ex-officio), Lewic, Mclntyre, Aaron, J. Hall, J. Baguley. P. Hall, J. W. Baguley, Priestner, Pick- ering, Brandreth, Parr. H. Linaker (clerk), and 11. G. Linaker (deputy clerk).

DE. MCDOUGALL AND THE FEVER HOSPITAL. The Clerk read the following letter from the Local Government Board :—Sir, I am directed by the Local Government Board to advert to the question raised in your letter of the 20th November with reference to the medical attendance upon pauper patients in the infec- tious Hospital belonging to the Runcorn Urban Sanitary Authority. The Board having given the matter their further consideration are of opinion that if a patient is removed to the Hospital and is unable himself, in conse- quence of his destitution, to obtain medical attendance, the Relieving Officer or the Guardians may properly give an order for the attendance of the District Medical Officer, in the case, and that it would be the duty of the Medrcal Officer to comply with such order. Your obed- ient servant, Edmund H. Woodhouse, assistant secret- ary."—Mr. Aaron asked if the Doctors would have to attend withont extra pay. The Clerk : Certainly. He added that he should send a copy of the letter to Dr, .McDougall.

div.head: COUNTY CALL.
div.p: THE COUNTY CALL.

The Clerk said he had received a precept from the Comity Council for the sum of £3,038 us. id. to be paid on or nefore the ninth of February. The amount was made up as folliws :—County rate, £1,847 is. Bd. ; constabulary general expenditure, £461 146. 11d. ; con- stabulary local expenditure, £727 14s. 6d. He remarked that this was £393 more than the Board had estimated for.
FrNANCE.
On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £246 19s. 7d. were passed for payment.
ALDERMAN 3IUSPRATT ON SABBATH OBSERVANCE.

Mr. Alderman Muspratt, of Widnes,took the chair at the meeting of the Liverpool Sunday Society, on Sunday last, and said he was glad to say that for the last thirty years a movement had been going on to bring about a change in the observance of the Sunday. Ile believed that that would contribute very much to the development of English music. When this Sunday movement began some thirty Years ago they heard a great deal about the Jewish Sabbath and about, the descretion of the Lord's Day. These were the arguments used by their opponents, and be was glad to say they had almost died away. They did not hear these arguments much now, but other arguments were introduced, and they were told that by recreation of that kind they entailed Sunday labour. Why, there was no people more earnest in endeavouring to lessen Sunday labour than the supporters of the Sunday Society. These gentlemen,who formerly were their opponents, who supported Sunday labour in public-houses (laughter), and who opposed the introduction of what they called the thin end of the wedge, bad told them that it would be introducing a Continental Sunday. Well, he had known the Continental Sunday for the last forty years, and what was the change going on on the Continent? The change was the diminution of Sunday labour—(hear, hear),--hut they did not intend to do away with Sunday recreation and rest. The only way in which they could enjoy perfect rest, was by recreation' by listening to delightful music and attractive lectures, or by strolling through picture galleries and the like and perusing works of art. The object of the Sunday Society in Liverpool was to further a movement of this kind. They had made some progress, but bad met with very considerable resistance. He (Mr. 3luspratt) hoped that in Liverpool they would have in a very few years not only the Rotunda Lecture Hall and the Art Gallery and Museum, but also the Free Library, opened to them. for entertainments such as they had just been enjoying. .(Applause.) RIVAL WORKMEN'S UNIONS. A SQUABBLE.

a general meeting of chemi- On Saturday evening, cal and other labourers, was held in the Dining- rooms, Victoria-road, Widnes, for the purpose of forming a branch of the St. Helens and District Labourers Union, At the time announced for the meeting, there was only a 6mail attendance, but later the number increased until there were nearly one hundred present. Among those present were a number of the Widnes members of the Chemical and Copper Workers Union, and there were also several members of the St. Helens branch of the same union. The chair was taken by one of the workmen. It was afterwards stated by Mr. J. Chadwick, the secre- tary, that he addressed the meeting at some length relative to the objects of the St. Helens and District Labourer's Union, and explained that that union was UV no means wishing to act in antagonism to the Chemi- cil and Copper Workers' Union which Mr. P. J. King had founded. There. was a large number of men unorga- nised in Widnes, and there was room for both organisa- tions to work. He wished that they would all work amicably together. He then invited any questions, and a number were asked and answered. Mr. Chadwick appeared to be irwensed at the behaviour of several of the members of the St. Helens branch of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, and there was some un- pleasantness for a time. Ultimately a resolution was passed that a branch of the Labourers Union be formed, and fifty persons gave in their names as members. A local secretary was appointed, and it was decided to hold another meeting to elect other officers.' At the Widnes railway station, later in the evening, there was a little scene. Several members of the rival unions met lathe waiting-room. lot words and some blows passed between them, tut fortunately the quarrel was not serious. It is stated that the result may be that one or two members of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union may make their appearance in the police court. On Monday night Mr. P. J. King, the president of the Chemical and Copper Workers Union, addressed a meet- ing of the executive committee, at the British Lion, Church-st.. St. Helens. In the course of his remarks, he referred to the meeting he on Saturday night, at
THE ENGINES OF SHIPS AND OF MEN.

In the month of March, the great and beautiful steam- ship" City of Paris," while on her voyage from New York to Liverpool, met with an accident by which her engines were completely disabled, leaving her helpless on the sea. She carried a large number of passengers, and great anxiety was felt concerning her, in Europe and America. 'flow she was finally towed into Queenstown Harbour will be remembered by the public. "Well, what of it ?" you say. "They afterwards found out how it happened, and repaired the engines,and

no lives were lost." Very true, but wait a moment. Because youlnever go to sea, do you think the sudden destruction of a ship's engine has no lesson for you? How shortsighted men are I Did you ever lie on your bed at home, or on a cot in a hospital, helpless as a dog? What ailed you? Some . _
disease. What is disease It is an accident to .your vital machinery. What do the doctors try to do for you?

To " Cure " you. Yes, of course. Suppose we say "repair "you ; it mimes to the same thing ; for we are kept alive and going by certain organs or engines inside the body. When they are out of order, and work badly, we are ill ; when they stop, we die. Do you see the force of the illustration? Sometimes a man's machinery is never right from the hour of his birth. Here is a short story one man tells about himself, which will show what we mean. He says: "One ship is never weak because another is; but a baby may be week because its parents were, or some Other of its ancestors. 'lt is spoken of in the family that, when I was an infant, I did notning but sleep. Now, a healthy infant ought to sleep most of the time, but not all the time. He'should laugh, play. cry, kick, and take notice of things. My- mothes was bothered about it, and saw the doctor, who said it was owing to the sluggish state of my liver. Nevertheless, hived and grew up as millions of children do. But inherited disease makes its mark sooner or later, according to circumstances. "About five years ago I began to feel bad. I didn't know what was the matter with me, I had a bad taste in -my mouth, a slimy tongue,and felt languid aaid•tired, and had no ambition for work. My appetite failed, and when I did eat, under a sort of compulsion, I had great pain after it. I went on in this way until the spring of 1888, when I had a very severe attack, and was treated in Bartholomew's Hospital for some time. But I came out still weak, and a little lateron I Was S.) bad 'broke down completely, and took to my bed. Matters now looked very serious for me. • "The first doctor who came to see me was not able to give any relief, and my people fetched another, as my condition had become alarming. I got worse, and was in great agony. I had pains all over me, but more particularly in the bowels, where the pain was intense, The bowels were stepped or constipated, and the doctor seemed puzzled. One day he said, I cannot account for your condition? I now began to think what was best to be done. Yet what could I do? "I had heard of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. which wassaid to be a most remarkable cure for deep-seated aud chronic complaints where all other remedies were unavailing, but I had never tried it, and why should I believe in it ? Yet how strangely we 'are sometimes led into paths we have never travelled before ! "About this time I picked up a newspaper, and read of a case similar to.my own that had been cured—so the writer said—by Mother Seigel's Syrup. I decided to risk it, and sent over to Mr. Dyer, the chemist, in Acre-lane, West Rixton, and got a bottle, and in ten minutes after taking the fest dose I felt relief. "In my excitement and satisfaction I declared, This is the right thing! "After taking six bottles I found myself in perfeet health. lam a new min. I never was in better health in my life, and all the members of my family think of nay cure as all the more wonderful owing to my having suffered with liver complaint from my infancy. I will gladly answer any inquiries about Mother Seigel's Syrup, and what it did for me." (Signed) W. Goldspink, 126, Acre Lane, Brixton, and 19, Tachbrook Street, Pimlico. Mr. Goldspink is a pork butcher, and is well known and highly respected. In addition to his inherited weakness of the liver he suffered from deep-seated in- digestion and dyspepsia, with an acute attack of,con- stipation, a dangerous and often fatal complication. For this almost universal malady—often mistaken for other diseases Seigel's Syrup is the only remedy to be relied upon. Look in the papers an read the testimony of witnesses from John O'Groat's to Land's End.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

THE NUISANCE COMPLAINED OF BY COUNCILLOR DIXON At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Friday, Thomas McGuire and William Richardson, were charged with being disorderly, on the night of the nth inst., in Sankey-st. The offence consisted of that recently complained of to the Bench by Councillor Dixon, and was committed near his house.—Alderman Harrison said it was a nuisance that ought to be put a Stop to.—John Smallwood, was charged with the like offence close by in Arpley-st., on the same night. The three defendants were fined the costs, 3s. 6d. each, but the Bench intimated that in future such cases would be dealt with much more severely. STEALING PROM A CLOTHES LINE. At the Warrington_ Police Court, on Friday, garah Gavin and Mary McComb, of 4, Friars-lane, were - charged with stealing from the back yard of John Bolton, 7, Clare-st., a blue flannel, value 2,5. 6d., or receiving the Same knowing it to have been stolen.—Harriet Boltoa deposed that on Wednesday night, about 6.30, she missed the singlet from the line. She identified the singlet produced.—Detective-Sergeant Monaghan said he in company with Constable Smith went to McComb's house and asked her about the singlet. At first she said she knew nothing about it, but he brought her to the Police Station, and she said she had bought a singlet for 4d. front Mrs. Gavin, who had sent out for two pints of beer for the 4d. Gavin was also taken into custody.— Gavin who now made her 23rd appearance, her previous conviction having been for stealing a singlet, was now committed for a month's harp labour ; and there being a doubt in Mrs. Comb's case, the Bench gave her the bene- fit of it, and discharged her. . ASSAULT ON A WOMAN AT MOORE. A young Runcorn man, named John Cunliffe who was said to be of respectable parentage, was on Tuesday brought before the Daresbury bench of magistrates on a charge of assaulting Mary Ambrose, a young married woman. Mrs. Ambrose's husband is employed on the Ship Canal at Moore. On Saturday she had been to Warrington, but returned to Moore by the 5.17 p.m. train. She was making her way home when she met the prisoner and another young man, both of them ap- pearmg to be drunk. As soon as she got near Ounliffe he flung an arm round her neck and attempted to lift her clothes. She screamed, and the man who was with him pulled Cunliffe away. Prisoner pleaded guilty, and expressed penitence for his action. He had been given drink, which so completely upset him that he did not know what he was doing: A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed, or afortnight's imprisonment. CHARGE OF BRUTAL ASSAULT IN A RAILWAY CARRIAGE. At the Wa rrington Borough Police Court on Wednesday, William Williams, of Liverpool, was charged with assaulting John Lecumber, of the same place, in a rail- way carriage on Saturday night last. The prosecutor said he was 30ttrr1eving by the 9.45 train from Manchester to Liverpool on Saturday night last. He entered the train at Manchester under the impression that it started at 9.30, and waited in the carriage. The moment the train left Manchester the defendant entered the carriage. Witness had had a business dispute with the defendant, and had told him he would have no further communica- tion with him except in writing. The defendant on entering the carriage said " You now, and there is no one to interfere with me. Unless you give me £5 for Mr. Roberts's watch, I will kill Witness said "To begin with, I have not got £5, and, secondly, if I had I would not give you it. There is a proper place to make the demand in. not a railway carriage." Immediatelfafter the defendant struck him between the eyes. He said "Now, you shall have two black eyes to begin with." Then witness received a blow on the side of his head, and tlows round the body, and he became unconscious. Defendant seized him by the throat, and tried to open the doer to throw him out- side. Witness seized the handle to prevent him opening the door, and a scuffle took place all the way to Warring- ton. What brought witness to consciousness was a blow at the side of the head, a very stunning blow. Then he found the train slackening speed, and he jumped out al- most before the train stopped at Warrington, and *told the station officials to give the defendant in charge. Witness was injured inwardlyond his wrists were in- jured in defending his face.—The defendant: Didn't you say if I had a piece of black lead you would give me £5 and settle for the watch you stole, and which you thought at the time I had a warrant out for P—The pro- secutor: No. The only thing I remember is you said, "I have followed you about all day, and now I have you, and (to the Bench) evidently he had been following me about all clay.—The defendant said he had not. He had been on business to Rochdale and was just coming back. When he got into the carriage the defendant was fast asleep. hr about a quarter of an hour the defendant asked him to settle about a watch he bad sold to Mr.
Roberts. The prosecutor got up in a rage' and the de- fendant just touched him with the backof his hand.

The prog.cutor was drunk in the railway carriage.—A booking clerk deposed that he rode in the adjoining car- riage from Manchester to Warrington, and heard no row or scuffling. The complainant got out at Warrington, and shouted for some one to lock the defendant up. Both were under the influence of drink, but neither was drunk.—The defendant was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months and ordered to pay costs.

RUFFIANLY ASSAULT ON A WARRINGTON CONSTABLE. At the Warrington" Borough Police Court on Wednes- day, George Hopkins, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Turner in the execu- tion of his duty on Tuesday night, and rescuing a pri- soner from his custody, in Scotland-road. P.C. Turner said he was on duty in Buttermarket-st., on 'ruesday night, when a young man came to him and said he was living at Daley's lodging-house in Scotland-road, and a young manhad robbed him of 4d. in the back yard of that house. Witness accompanied him there, and he picked out the prisoner's brother as the man who had robbed him. Witness apprehended the man, and he came away very quietly, but when he got into Scotland-road, he said "Now, you I will go nq further. I have gone far enough," aild struck him a violent blow on the side of the head, then butted him. Witness closed with him and got him down. The prisoner here came up and kicked witness in the ribs and in the fore- head. He struggled with them for bout ten mimutes, and blew his whistle, but no assistance came for a long _while. Witness stuck to them as long as he could, but both got away. He followed them up Town Hill, and he got Hopkins. A young man came to witness's assis- tance,and with great difficulty they brought the prisoner to the station. He gave witness a black eye and damag3d his nose, and said to the other prisoner, "Kick the—'s guts in and murder him. —John Brown, County Court bailiff, also gave evidence, and in reply to the Chief-Constable, the witness said the wound on the prisaner's head was caused by his falling to the ground. The officer never drew his staff, though witness requested him to do so, but hit the man with his fists. Turner at witness's request put the "snaps" on the man.—ln answer to the prisoner the witness said he heard nothing of the crowd shouting "Don't murder the man. You have hit him two or three times w'th the handcuffs

across the face." The prisoner nromised to take the pledge and never drink more, if the Bench would let him off, but his present appearance was his 22nd, and the Chairman said they must make an example of him for such conduct, as the police must belzotected ; and he was sent to prison for two months' hard labour. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY • AND A STRANGE TALE OF ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.

Edward Burke was charged at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tuesday with being drunk and disorderly soon after midnight that morning, also with assaulting Charlotte Pritchard, in Napier-street, about the same time.—Pritchard said she came from Horwich, near Bolton, the previous night with some friends. She went into a public-house and had a glass of beer, and the defendant awl some other men came in. She paid

for a good deal of drink, and they said they would- tie° her right for a night's lodging and something to eat. He said he would take her home to his mother's house, but he had no house to take her to, and took her down by the river, brought her up a back street And abused her, and threw her against a wall, coming out with very bad language. He said if she had not been in such a state he would have done something more. She was married and had seven children. She screamed out but could get nobody to hear her, and he put her arms against her mouth and threatened what he would do if she did not hush. She had left her husband because they had some words. He would know now where she was. The defendant knocked her across the face and hit her across the shoulder. She did not know why he assaulted her.—Cross-examined by the defendant, she denieu that she was drunk in the public- house and that she clipped a young man sayijig he was just like her brother.—The defendant: You could not walk you was that drunk. Yon wanted me to go on the road with you out of the town last night.—The prosecutrix: I! what an untruth !—P.C. 17 deposed that at 12 o'clock the previous night, the prosecutrix complained to him in Mersey-st that the defendant had been abusing her in Napier-st., and had thrown her down and tried to kiss her. While she was tehing him, the defendant came up, and he was drunk and disorderly. Sha had had a glass of beer, but knew what she was dding.—P.C. 19 corroborated as to the defendant being drunk asd dis- orderly.—The defendant said he had been knocked off a form in the station by an officer. He was as innocent of the charge as the Bench tv‘emselves. She treated him to a quart and because she did so wanted him to find her lodgings and take her on the road. He was committed for 14 days' hard labour, but the Chairman called up the prosecutrix and told her her story wasnot a very straight one, and her leaving her husband and seven children to come to Warrington for no earthly Purpose and then going into a public-house as she did was disreputable. She did not deserve any sympathy whatever. A LANDLADY AND LODGER'S DIFFERENCE.—CHICKEN SOUP SERVED IN A WASII-RASIN.—At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Harry Manton, stage manager at the Empire Theatre of Varieties, Sankey-st., appeared to answer a summons issued at the instance of Mrs. Rachel Ravenscroft, theatrical lodginsshouse keeper, Friar's-green, who charged him with 'lying assaulted her on the 23rd inst. A cross-summons alleged that Mrs. Ravenscroft assaulted Manton.—Mr. A. B owne, solici- tor, who appeared for Mrs, Ravenscroft, said that the defendant and his wife went to lodge at the house of his client some five weess ago, but had not yet paid any-- thing for their lodgings. Between ten and eleven o'clock on Friday night, when there were only Mrs. Ravenscroft and a servant in charge of the house, the alleged assault was' committed, and it appeared, Mr. Browne said, that there was a conspiracy, not only to get the defendant's goods out of the house' but to seriously assault her. Defendant had been upstairs several days, supposed to be ill, and on Friday night five men came to the house and went upstairs to his room. Mrs. Ravenscroft heard a rumbling noise, and then discovered that they were bringing downstairs the luggage of the defendant. Mr. Manton asked complainant for some articles of his cloth- ing, and she refused to give them up unless he ssttled the bill. Defendant then put his fist in her face,said she might "fancy shelled got" the money, and ordered the other men to smash open the door and throw her out." Th!s, it was alleged, was done, Mrs. Ravenscroft being dragged by the hair, thrown down the steps, and ren- derel unconscious.—Complainant and her servant gave -evidence in support of this statemcnt.—Defendant said said that on Monday he was at work at the Empire Theatre, and strained his back. He had to be taken to his lodgings and put to bed, as he was very ill. After that Mrs. Ravenscroft continually grumbled at having a sick man in the house, and refused to let them have the use of cooking utensils. In conSeqnence they had to have chicken soup served in a wash-basin. Defendant ultimately sent for friends, who procured him fresh lodgings, and went on Friday night to assist him to re- move. He was still so ill as to be unable to dress him- self, and denied having touched the complainant. On the contrary, she struck him. He admittee that by his orders a door was forced open, but said that was the only way by which he could get his clothing and leave the house. He entirely repudiated Mrs. Ravenscroft's bill, and alleged that she had been paid weekly. After hearing several witnesses for the detence, the Bench dismissed both summons and cross-summons, ordering each party to pay their own costs.—The male defepdant asked the magistrates to order the remaining goods to be given up to him.—Alderman Harrison said if he owed the landlady anything he had better pay her, because she had a lien on what she had belonging to him.—The defendant denied that he owed her anything.—Alderman Harrison said it would then be a question for another court.

SMASHING HER BROTHER'S WINDOW.--Sarall Robertson, of 56, Winwick-st., was charged with wilfully damaging the window of her brother, William Hollows, on Wednes- day night last. The prosecutor said that on the night in question, between 7and 8, he heard a knock at the door, and on going to it, he found the defendant there. He asked her what she wanted there, and she commenced to shout. He did not want her there and he shut the door. As soon as ho did so the stone (produced) came through his window. If it had come two or three inches further it would have broken the paraffin lampancl set fire tc the house.—The defendant said her mother told her that the prosecutor had been to her house abusing her in most oppr,bious terms, and defaming her character. As he had done this several times she went to see him about it, and he so provoked her that she threw the stone through the window.—The prosecutor said hehad'only used to his mother words repeated to him by the defendant herself. She was ordered to pay co.sts and damages together 7s 6d.
