RUGBY. STOCKTON HERM V. HALTON VIEW.—ThiS match was played at Stockton Heath on Saturday, both 'teams being poorly represented, The visitors winning. tha toss, the home iream kicked off, and Soon registered a minor. After the drop-out the 110040 team again pressed, and Itathbone scored after a grand run, no goal result- ing. At half-time the score stood—Stockton Heath, 1 try,•l minor, to 1 minor. In tha second half the home
team' had the best of matters throughout, Lingard scor- ing after a series of scrimmages on the line, and shortly _ .

afterwards Risley crossed th-e line, E. Twiss converting. After this nothing nothing but minors were scared, and the home team finally won by 1 goal 2 tries and 5 minors to 1 minor. WARRINGTON v. MANCHESTErt RANGERS. For the past five weeks football in the Warrington dis-
trict has been at a standstill, and the practical re-opening of the season on 'Saturday was welcomed by all lovers of

the game in this district. Although the day was adverse to the allowing of a good game, there would be over three thousand assembled when the teams turned out, but then the Rangers' reputation of playing a pure open game in some measure accounted for this. The heavy rain of the previous day and a few hours before the match had ren- dered the ground in a sloppy Condition, and as the play during the first half was confined, to this quarter, the amusement reached a high pitch. It was nearly 3.30 before Frank Turner kicked off to- wards the pavilion goal, and although a poor reply was effected, Pollard and Parlane were instrumental in plac- ing the game at neutral ground. The brothers Turner were foremost in a rush which terminated in a scrimmage near the Rangers' line, but the defence, assisted. by the' water, which lay in large pools of two to three inches in depth, was stubborn. From a line out, the smart Rangers took-the oval out of danger, and J. T. Bate passed finely to Barnes, but the greasy nature of the' oval caused a mull. However, a smart display of passing by the home back, was frustrated by Sabin, who smartly tackled Webster before he could fairly get in his stride. Fair Turner next got clear from a line out and passed grandly across to Massey, who punted to near the' line, but Bull managed to clear. The visitors pluckily responded, and

Lloyd,Hasleham, and Comman dribbled effedtively to the centre flag. The home forwards, conspicuous amongst others being Ashton and Berry, assisted by their clever half backs, soon had the oval back to its original position. Evans and Jolley were alinost in after a grand effort. 'Okell was specially prominent in staving off a welhmeant effort to score by the right wing, and a movement initia-

ted by James Bate was-followed by some sharp tactics in several line-outs by J. T. Bate, Berry, Donohue, and, Holmes. The oval was kept on the go, and after Webs- ter had once more made a strong attempt to score, the oval was sent over the line, and Ashton, despite the water amidst the laughter of the home enthusiasts, crossed—or rather waded—the line and scored the first point to War- rington, Fair Turner with a beautiful kick increasing the value of the point. From the re-start Pearson made his mark under difficulties, and a fine piece of play between J. T. Bate, Frank Turner, and E. Dillon ,led up to Ashton scoring again, but the point was negatived owing to some infringement. The Manchester men changed the venue, and Boscow was called upon for the first Lisle. but Webster and Fair Turner soon had the ball back, and James Bate slapped at a moment when the goal was at his mercy. The two Batesagain demonstrated what clever players they are by a series of short passes, which almost ended in a score, and play was in the visitors' lines when half time was called, with War- rington leading by one goal. Ilasleha:n re-started, and the Rangers by a combined rush took the oval under the Warrington posts. This .determined rush of the visitors had evidently taken the Warringtpnians by sur- prise, for a moment later saw our local team forcing their way down the open, Evans, Holmes, Berry, Jolley and Ashton leading the way until the oval was close on, the line, a judictus kink by Taylor saving his side from disaster. The oval, was worked across the field by a series of passes; and Fair Turner got an apparently legitimate try, but fortune favoured the homesters a moment later, for a neat display of short passes by the half backs resulted in Barnes running strongly and scoring near the posts, the easy place failing. The re- start was met by J. T. Bate, and although only a poor reply was effected, Evans' by an excellent run, again his opponents in a defensive attitude. A grand chance was ingloriously missed by the Warringtonians through their over-eagerness to score, and some mulling gave the Rangers some chance to relieve, which they gladly accepted. Boscow was equal to the task imposed on him, and a fine kick made the visitors beat a hasty retreat. Berry and Barnes led up a dribble to the line,and Holmes, working the oval grandly with his toes, scored under the posts,Turner this time landing a goal. Follow- ing this came some fine work by James Bate, and after he had succesfully _shone in several movements, a fine Ctrlbbl6 by this promising half-back sent the oval past Bull, and Barnes and Massey being well up, the oval was gathered excellently by the former, and the last try of the match scored, Fair Turner landing a goal. Towards the close Frank Turner put in an exact dribble, but danger WaS averted by Sabin, and the whistle brought the game to a conclusion, the final score reading as follows :—Warrington, 3-1-0; Manchester Rangers, nil. " Teams: Warrington :. J. Boscow, back; J. W. Evans, T. Barnes, J. T. Massey (captain), and H. Webster three- quarter backs; J. T. Bate and James Bate, half backs; H. Ashton, Fair Turner:, Frank Turner, E. Dillon,Hohnes, W. Berry, T. .Donohue, and J. Jolley, forwards. Man- chester Rangers: W. Bull, back; Taylor, W. G. Sabin, and T. Okell, three-quarter backs: W. Parlane and M. Bogg, half backs; Herbert Hasleham, G. Pollard, E. Mee, W. Pearson, T. Comman, R. Ashton, Westbrook, Lloyd, and Rowe, forwards. Referee, • Mr. H. Lord, Broughton. • "

Sunderland was charged down, his leg being, broken in two places. Notts can ill spare him in view of the Cur/ ties. They were beaten by four goals. The North End were too good for Aston Villa at Preston, and Burnley did good work in finishing in front of Derby County, on the ground of the last-named.

The rumoured dissensions in the League caused no slight commotion. They sprang out of a movement initiated by a member of the Accrington club, who finis that visits by Midland teams do not pay. There is really a project on foot for the establishmnt of "a Northern League, but it is not likely to meet with much support. The original League has been such a marked success in many ways that its present members may be trusted to remain loyal, and there is not room for two organisations of a first-rate character.

Great indignation is said to prevail at Accrington, in consetuence of the name of the Accrington club being so freely associated with the reported split in the Foot- ball League. It is affirmed that Mr. Critchley, the con- vener of the meeting of Lancashire clubs represents himself only, and some of the Accrington club have been SO irritated by his conduct that they have requisitioned the committee to call a general meeting to consider the club's position in the matter.

WARRINGTON (ASSOCIATION) V. WESTERN POINT..I—ThiS match took place on the club ground at Arpley. The teams faced each other shortly after three o'clock, the ground being in fairly good condition. The visitors kicked off with the wind in their favour, and at once made tracks for the home goal, but could not break through the grand defence of the home team. The home loft then made tracks for goal, and Mather passed to Carnforth, that player missing an easy goal. Play began to range in mid.field, the whistle sounding for half-time, no goals being scored. Carnforth re-started and the, home team commenced in earnest, Simkins putting in a grand shot, the goalkeeper saving at the expense of a fruitless corner. The visitors' right then broke away, Parry pulling up grand, and after a splendid bit of pass- ing among the bcme ranks, Simkins headed across to Clayton and he with a well-directed 'shot scored; putting his side ahead. The visitors woke up after this, but the half-back play of Ayling.Simkins, and Parry was impreg- nable. Give and take play foll Owed for a bit till Mather getting possession passed to Clayton he hitting the cross- bar with his final shot. The home team continued to have the best of the play the whistle sounding for time. Final reoult : Warrington, 1 goal; Weston Point nil. This was a very creditable victory as the Weston Point heat the Cheshire Juniors' Cup Holders by 3 goals to L There was a marked improvement all round. div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.

ASB.OCIATION. The re-played cup ties furnished another surprise in the overwhelming defeat of the Bolton Wanderers, at Ac- crington. Nobody was prepared for a five goals to one triumph for the Reds, but they were far and away the smarter team. The Baltonlans were terribly slow on the mud-covered ground,and could not cope at all with their small opponents.' The nimbleness of the home represen- tatives on such an enclosure was really extraordinary. 'The slush and filth seemed to make little difference to them, whilst on the other hand the visitors could not get along. The backs were all at sea and could not stop the rushes of the Accrington front rank. Barbour, of the Wanderers' team, was sent off the ground by the referee, the offence alleged against him being that he struck Pen- dergast, but this was-stoutly denied.. Barbour is one of the most respected of professional- footballers, and every- body seemed to be sorry fpr him.

The cupholders made no mistake on their Second visit to Middlesbrough, when they knocked out Ironopolis by threeto none. Kidderminster had no chance whatever on the shockingly bad ground at Damen, and the locals ran round them to the tune of 13 goals to none. St. George's again joorneyed up to London, and accounted for the last„,of the southerners, though they were only two goals better than the Crusaders. The ties which are set down for to-day (Saturday) should produce some keen contests. The best will probably be at Sunderland, where the Albion will be opposed by Notts Forest. The Clubs met in an Alliance fixture at Nottingham last Satur- day v. hen each side scored a goal. The Rovers are very lightly drawn with Chester, who are not likely to shine at Ewood Park.

div.p: FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

Taking the previous matches between Lancashire and Durham as a criterion, there was not much hope for the visitors to Whalley Range on Saturday. Since the counties first met in 1886, the northeners had not once been suc- cessful, though they managed to draw with their oppo- nents at Hartlepool three years ago. Lancashire have been going so well this season that they were generally expected to add to their list 6lf successes, and the expect- tation was fully borne out. The pity was that the surroundings were so miserable, the players being placed at a great disadvantage by the drenching rain and the fearfully heavy ground. The Wonder is that the teams did so well, as to get about at all was a work of extreme difficulty. The prospect of Lancashire being finally hailed champions of the season seems to brighten every time they turn out.

Two goals and a try represented the extent Of the vic- tory of Yorkshire over Somersetshire. The ground at Bradford was all against good play, telling severbly against the visitors, who are more accustomed to a fast turf. Their forwards proved tab° a very capable lot. S. M. J. Woods, the international, was an admirable model, Hancock also being prominent. Barnes, of Hali- fax, made a creditable full back, a goal he-placed from a difficult position, being a very fine bit of work.
THE DISTRESS IN WA RRINGTON.

DISCUSSION AT THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS, TRADE GOOD AND TIIE DISTRESS EXAGGERATED. At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians OR Wednesday it was reported that there had only been 28 applications for the allowanqe of school fees, a number much smaller than usual. A report bearing on the alleged exceptional distress in the town, which had been submitted to the School Attendance Committee by Mr. Shearer, attendance officer, was also read as follows : " It occurred to me that it would be interesting to compare the number of applications for school fees for the three meet- ings during the recent hard weather with the num- ber during the same period in past years. and I find that the applications are considerably fewer "this winter than any winter since 1884. For the three meetings in Deeember and January, 1885-6, we allowed 166 cases; 1886-7, 167 cases; 18874, 134; 1888-9, 118.; 1889-90, 99; and 1890-1,80 cases, or less than one half of those alloWed in 1886 and 1887, and 19 less than last year. I have found very few cases of actual destitution, but those who are in this condition have suffered very much during the frost. As far as I can see, the forges, wire-works, factories and fustian-cutting shops have not been working so regular for many years during the winter months as they have been this winter. Many out-door labourers have some member or members of their families employed in one or another of these works, and this I consider has enabled them to pull through without assistance."—The CtrainnrlN (Alderman Harrison) asked Mr. Shearer if he based his impres- sions upon the applications for school fees.—Mr. SHEARER said he did partly and partly upon what he saw when visiting. Ile visited every ease where there was an application, and he was visiting or inquiring for money almost every . day in the week. Whenever he heard of a case of poverty he inquired into it and if he thought relief was needed he sent the people to the relieving officers. The exper- ience of the relieving officer had been the same as his, and Mr. Harbourne said he had a less number of cases than last year.—The GnAssaaarr did not think the reliev- ing officers, no matter what care they exercised, could form a complete opinion as to the amount of distress that prevailed. He mentioned an instaneein which Mrs. Harrison had visited a house in which a man sat by the expiring embers of a fire, with bare feet, his shoes hav- ing been pawned. Mrs. Harrison asked him why he did , not applyto the Board of Guardians and he replied that he had applied to the Board two years ago, but they wanted to send him into the Workhouse with his wife and' family . • As he only wanted relief for a few weeks he did not think it worth while breaking up his house. Mrs. Harrison then asked him why he did not apply for relief in the shape of food, and he replied that he did not know that he could do that. There were many people in the same position, and therefore a relieving officer could not form an opinion.—Mr. SHEARER said that respectable families who had conducted themselves in the.past as they should do, found no difficulty in get- ting trust at the small shops. He instanced the case of the boatmen, irom whom the Guardians had never had an application. He supposed they got credit, and thus tided over the difficulty. He pointed out also that the charitable were sometimes imposed upon, and said that he once visited a man who had rolled himself in a sack because he said his trousers had been pawned: He (Mr. Shearer) did not suppose the trousers had been pawned, and he told the man that they could do nothing for him unless he found his trousers, and-he then soon found the trousers. (Laughter.) There were some people who did that sort of thing if they thought they could get anything by it.—The CLERK (Mr. J. Sutton) 'said that many of those people found that unless they put on an appearance of abject poverty they .would get no sympathy. There was a good deal of imposition and misrepresentation, and he could not help thinking when he heard the statement of the chairman with regard to the man whose boots had been pawned that the boots might have been disposed of so that the man might not be called upon to do any work. He then alluded to the" statement that the Corporation of Warrington had found great difficulty in getting men at 2s. 6d. a day to clear the streets of snow. Although they had 'seventy men the first day only seventeen turned up the next day, and scarcely any on the third day. In his experience he had known of many instances similar to that of the men in the sack. With regard to a large part of the chronic poverty in the town, it arose, in his judgment, from the fact that many of the people would not work in August let alone at Christmas. He was very sorry to read in a Liverpool paper of the.destitution said to be prevail- ing in Warrington. When lie remembered that ail the works in the town were going and that trade was in so good a state that there was ample employment, except for thohe people engaged out of doors, he did think it was scarcely the right thing that they should be made to appear in the county of Lancashire, and throughout the whole country, as being in such a state of distress. He thought it was a mistake to put it in such an exaggera- ted form in connection with Warrington. He had noticed a statement that the Board of Guardians were restricted in the administration of relief. It was time they were restricted in some respects, but the proper test of relief—and lie thought they would say it was a wise test—was the workhouse' and at that vvorkhous they had over 100 beds to spare and 50 beds at the schools. Having referred to the measure taken by the Guardians to make the workhouse and the schools comfortable for the inmates, the clerk added that if their great grandfathers could come again on this earth and see the kind of provision made at that Workhouse and at Padgate schools for people who had nothing to pay the thing would seem to them incredible. He believed that the sort of help that was now needed by destitute people was the help that required them to help them- selves. Nothing could be more generous than the action of those people who tried to ameliorate the condition of the poor, but it would be better it they would introduce into their system of procedure that kind of charity which they found laid down in the new Testament which said that though they bestowed all their goods on the poor if, without charity it profiteth not. The kind of charity that was wanted was that which gave the poor the opportunity of employment, to help them to take care of themselves as far asthe necessities of life went. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN said that no doubt at times like these the amount of distress was very much exagger- ated, but the principal sufferers were the children. Be- cause parents were improvident and pawned their goods was no reason why the children should continue in a state of starvation, and the relief that had been given at the Warrington Drill Hall had been almost exclusively confined to children. In answer to a question by the Chairman as to the small number of tramps who had called at the workhouse lately, the WORKHOUSE Masa= said there was no doubt that the tramp wards had been exceptionally cold during the winter owing to the heat- ing apparatus having gone wrong. New heating arranop- ments were, however, being provided.—The CLERK after- wards mentioned that there were that morning 292 inmates in the Workhouse as compared with 346 and 381 at the corresponding periods of two Previous years. He had also seen it stated that at the Runcorn Union Work- house there was not a tingle able-bodied inmate.—The discussion then dropped. MEETING OF THE RELIEF COMMITTEE. A meeting of the Temporary Relief Committee was held in the Mayor's Parlour, at the Town Hall, on Satur- day morning, the Mayor in the chair. There were also

present the Mayoress (Mrs. Francomb), Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Whittle, Mrs. J. L. Tunstall, Mrs. Smethurst, Mrs. Carleton, Miss Pierpoint, and Miss Kendrick; Aldermen Sutton, Wright, and Harrison ; the Rev. E. C. E. Cane- tot's the Revs. Fathers Feeny and Larkin. Mr. X- Lyon Wtittle (town clerk) ; Councillor Edward Greenall, and M . George Pilling, S. Jones, James Smethurst, and Pater Chrimes. A discussion took plaec as to the advis- ability-of continuing the relief, and it was decided, as the suggestion of Alderman Harrison, that the free din- ners be continued or another week, and that the Mayor be requested to appeal to the public for subscriptions. - Since the meeting-on Saturday, his Worship has-issued a circular in. which he says-:—We opened a SCap kitchen in the Drill' Hall, on Wednesdaylast, and hare already given 4,solMinners to poor and destitute children: The food has been eaten in our presence, and it was heart- rending to see some of the pinched feature,- of the little ones. We intend continuing the-dinners until next Saturday, when the men who have been eut of work will receive their first wages, since the starting of the- frost, about seven vreeks ago. We don't ask for a large sub- scription ,but if you will kindly help us we shall feel deeply thankful." A generous response has been made to the appeal, the largest subscriber being the Mayor,. £13,55. Gilbert Greenall, £5 (first donation) ;:Committee of the Treat to the Aged Poor £5 (first donation) ; Mr. R. Davies, £5; Mr. William Sharp,.E.3 3s. (first donation) ; Miss Pierpoint, £2'; Messrs. G. and J. Greenall £22; Messrs. Peter Walker • and Son, £5: (Ist donation) ; Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and C0.,.£5 ; Mr. John Fair- clough, £2 2s. Each day at noon(including S'unday),a free dinner has been given to the poor children of the town. An average of over 1,000 . per day have been, provided withdinner during the week, and yesterday those who sat down exceeded that ntimber. The Mayor has- been present daily superintending the operations, and, among those who have been present are the Mayoress, who has taken an active part in the distribution of the food, and a number of ladies and gentlemen most of whom' per- fermed a like part, including the Revs. E: C. E Carle- ton, H. V. Pigot, Fathers Feeney, Larkin, and Dolan, and the members of the Aged People's Treat Committee.

Police-Sergeants Taylor awl Cheney and several con- stables have also rendered assistance, some of them, who have been employed in cutting bread no doubt finding that the dispensing of the staff of life was better than the dispensing of that other staff to which they are accustomed. The Mayor informs us that through Police- Sergeants Taylor and Jones he has made inquiries with a view to ascertaining what cases of unrelieved distress; and what cases of pretended poverty •among the parents- of the children attending the soup kitchen existed,.with a view to the relief of the former and the prosecution if possible of the latter, but that not at single case of imposition was discovered. The Mayor has described some most pitiful tales of the misery and distress ex- empliied by some of the poor adults who have been relieved at the soup kitchen in addition to the children. One woman carried concealed under her shawl a baby which had absolutely not a vestige of clothing, upon it, and another woman brought with her an infant which had nothing on except a white handkerchief round its neck. To-day, the last of the dinners will be given, and it is probable that before the close of the soup kitchen the Mayor and others will have some public remarks to make on the subject of the distress.

div.head: TIIE THEFT EPIDEMIC.
div.p: TIIE THEFT EPIDEMIC.
At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on .Saturday, before Alderman Burgess (chairman), Councillor Voisey, and Mr. R. Garnatt, William Benjamin was charged

with being found, the previous night, in possessioii-of 5 lbs. of bacon supposed to have been stolen.—P.C. Evans deposed : —About 6-55 p.m. on the 23rd, he saw the prisoner in the neighbourhood of the Cemetery, try- ing to sell 5 lbs. of bacon, value 3s. 4-d. Witness asked him "Whose is that bacon ?" and he said" It's mine." Witness said" Where did you get it? and he replied "I bought it a week ago in Liverpool, and gave 2s. 3d. for it." Witness brought lihn to the police station and " charged him, and he answered "When a man is drunk he will buy anything in the shape of meat from any shop that he comes across." Witness made inquiries at a lodg- ing-house at which the prisoner stayed on Thursday night, and the people there said he had not the bacon with him when he lodged at the house, which he left at half-past nine on Saturday morning. Witness had not found any owner for it.—The prisoner : The bacon is mine, and you can't find any man breathing to stand in front of me and say I have stolen it. I left the lodging-house yester- day morning with the bundle that had the bacon in it. I went to a house three miles off and tried to sell it, and the policeman saw me. —The prisoner was remanded. Bridget Burke, wife of Patrick Burke, 16, Union- street, was charged with stealing from a clothes-line, about six o'clock on the night of the • 21st inst., a man's woollen shirt, the property of John Madden. Mary Madden saw-the .hirt on the line about half-past five, and shortly after missed it. Information was given to the police, and the different clothes dealers,, and it app- peared that the prisoner had, on the 23rd inst., offered the shirt for sale at Mrs. Leslie's, Mersey-at., for ls.,and she immediately recognised the shirt as belonging to Mrs. Madden. Detective-sergeant Monaghan was sent for, and he apprehended the prisoner. She now said she was drunk at the time and did not know how the shirt came into her possession. The prisoner's husband, who was described as a steady, hard-working, man, and who is employed at Tinsley's tannery, said he and the children had been starved for the last nine weeks through his wife's drinking. About nine weeks since she was summoned by Mr. Norman for neglecting to keep her house in a proper sanitary condition, and 'ever , since she had been addicted to think, and the fine was

not paid ,yet. Still he tried his- best to to keep things together, and lost no time. He earned £1 a week, and had to pay Zs. 6d. a week out of t towards the fine, and he had three children. His-wife was never addicted to drink before being summoned.--The prisoner; My biain really turns sometimes, and I don't think what am doing. He lost three days at Christmas, and a day since.—The Chairman said if her husband lost this time, it was through circumstances over which he had no con- trol; and asked the prisoner how she came by a black eye she had got. She replied that her husband had given her it because she would not get him his tea. She pro- mised to sign the pledge if discharged.—Her husband; I have warmed her a bit.—The Chairman said this was a 'very painful case and a very difficult one to dispose of, but lithe Bench sent her to jail her young children and. her worthy husband would suffer through her miscon- duct. Therefore, this being her first offence, the court would be content with recording the conviction, to remain on the book against her incase she ever appeared again. The Chairman reminded her that She had pro-, Mised to sign the pledge, and asked her- husband to take her to Fattier Flannigan and see her sign it, and he promised to do so. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, Michael James Corney, a boy, aged 16, who came from Manchester, was charged with ;stealing, on the previous night, a man's blue serge jacket, value 2s. 6d., from the shop ef William Hudson, draper, Irlam-st. Mrs. Lucy Hudson, deposed to discovering that the-article had been stolen from within her shop door, and to the jacket pro- dticed being like it, but could not identify it.—The pri- soner, who pleaded guilty, said he had no father or mother and lost them three years \,ince.—Deteetive-Ser- geant Monaghan said on Monday night he was informed of the theft and apprehended prisoner and a younger boy who was with him, and under the former's clothes he found the jacket. The little boy said in the prisoner's presence that he told him to watch while he stole the Jacket. The prisoner had on him 6d. and a large quan- tity of bread, meat, and fish. He had been going about railway stations in Manchester carrying parcels, and sleeping in common lodging-houses.-The prisoner, in reply to the Chairman, said he had never been in jail before and had never attended a Sunday school. He was oa his way, when arrested,. to Ellesniere Port, to work on the Ship Canal, where he had worked before.—Detective- Sergeant Monaghan' at the request of the Bench, exam- ined the prisoner's hands, and said he did not appear 'to have been working.—Chief Constabla Hunt: How come you with such soft hands ?—The prisoner: It is such easy work sitting down by the fife.—ln reply to the Bench, he said he left Ellesmere Port, where he was earning 3id. an hour, to-go to Manchester with another lad.—The ' Chairman said the prisoner deserved.to be sent to jail, but a conviction would be recorded against him, and he would be kept at the station till a policeman had time to see him out of the town. The Chairman 'asked him if he would promise to steal no more.—The prisoner I will never steal any more.—The Chairman told him that stealing led to worse things, and he would end his days , on the gallows if ho went on with that sort of thing. If he was charged with anything else in future the present conviction would be brought up against him.—Chief ' Constable Hunt explained that nothing could be proved against the younger boy, and he had been taken to the Workhouse. • At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, before Mr. John White (chairman), Alderman Harrison, and Dr. Gornall, Thomas Mackie, from Handley, Staffordshire, was charged with stealing, on Wednesday, a pair of corded trousers, value ss. lid., from the shop of Valen- tine Morton pawnbroker, Winwick-street. The prisoner pleaded guilty. Chief Constable Hunt said the prisoner had been convicted before, and he would not ask ;he Bench to commit him for trial- now, but if he came up again, he would most likely do so.—Alderman Harrison: We must impose a penalty.—The Chief Constable: Oh, he has got no money.—The prisoner was committed for a month's hard labour.
The Nottingham TOwn Council decided on Monday to abolish the races which have been held every spring and autumn on the Forest raceepurse kr a hundred years. . _ _ _

The experts appointed by the Glasgow Town Council to inquire into the recent gasometer explosion, have found indications of some explosive having been placed on the crown of No. 2 gasholder. It has been decided to offer a reward of £l,OOO. FUNERAL OF PRINCE BALDWIN.

BRUSSELS, TUURSDAY.—Immense crowds gathered in the streets to witness Prince Baldwin's funeral. The procession proceeded from the Flanders Palace to Laekin, whew the corpse will be interred in the Royal crypt. The King, with Prince Albert,Count Flanders,and Prince henry of Germany attended the funeral service at Saint Gudulo, which was most impressively conductod, The King appeauira to suffer much. The day was, dry, though cloudy.

div.p: THE LATCHFORD RAILWAY FATALITY.
TAYLOR v. THE LONDON AND NORTH- WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

On Wednesday in the Court of Appeal, consisting of the Master of the Rolls and Lords Justices Bowen and Pry, the defendant company applied for a new trial in this action, in which the plaintiff, a widow, residing at Warrington, recovered £3OO damages at the Liverpool Assizes, for the loss of her husband, Who was killed on the London and North-Western 'Railway at Latchford Station, Lancashire, on the 6th April, 1889. Mr. Potter, Q.C., and Mr. Ernest Page (instructed by Mr. Mason, solicitor), appeared for the defendant company ; and Mr. Addison, Q.C., and Mr. E. W. Jordan (instructed by Mr. A. nexasdale, solicitor, of Longton), were counsel for the respondent. It appeared that the deceased husband of the plaintiff, Frederick Gray Taylor, was a traveller for a wine and ,BPlrit and beer firm, and on the fatal day when he lost Ws life he was crossing over the defendant company's line at Latchford, after having taken a ticket for Lymm, With two companions named Lambert and Howorth. It Was necessary for the deceased to cross the line to catch His train at the opposite platform to the booking office. Seeing what he thought was his train approach,he endea- voured to cross the line, and in doing so he received such severe injuries that he afterwards died. The company's 1 case was that there was no evidence of negligence to go ' to the jury, and that there should be a new trial if the court did not consider that the finding of the jury should be set aside altogether. The plaintiff's husband received t 2 a week wages and commission; and the defendant's counsel submitted that he had lost his life through his ?Wu recklessness and carelessness. The train by which ..ne 'was to travel had not arrived, and the one which 'mocked him down only consisted of an engine and a carriage or two. The Master of the Rolls„ without calling upon the learned counsel for the respondent, said there was plenty of evi dence in support of the charge of negligence made -against the company. There was ht, intimation sent by , the officials to Latchford stating that the engine with the 1 carriage which caused the death of the plaintiff's husband 1 Ivas coming through before the stopping train for Lymm. ' It was for the jury to say whether the company were (eUilty of negligence, having had all the facts 'before them. The application for a new trial must be dismissed With costs. Lords Justices Bowen and Fry concurred.

div.head: SHEEP WORRYING AT HAYDOCK.
div.p: SHEEP WORRYING AT HAYDOCK.

\V HOLES ALE DESTRUCTION.. A very bad case of sheep-worrying by dogs has taken place at llaydock, resulting in the destruction Of several sheep, and serious mutilation of others, belonging to Messrs. R. Evans and Co. On Thurs- day morning about eight o'clock, the shepherd employed by Messrs. Evans and Co. went in the . ordinary caurse of his-duties into afield belonging to the firm, known as Jib-road Field, and noticed two dogs, one a fox hound, and the other a black and tan Sheep dog, lurching in the Jib Wood.. There were a Uurober of sheep belonging to his employers in the field, and on going among them, he found that several of them had been much torn, one had an ear torn off, and another had its back completely torn to the flesh, and all the Nvaol pulled off, and others he found in a pit of water. kany of the sheep were so badly injured that they had - to be destroyed. On going to the Grange Field, where Other sheep were located, the , same condition of things was found to exist there, and some of the sheep there had to be destroyed, in consequence of their • %angled condition. Altogether the number destroyed by the dogs is seven, but many more will be rendered almost Useless, through having been chased and torn._ Police Constable Addison was furnished by the shepherd with a mescription of the dogs, and has pushed his enquiries with (t) ornmendable vigour and astuteness, with the result that ~.vvo dogs believed to be those in fault, and which have u"en recognised by the shepherd, have been discovered on a farm at Garswoocl. A report of the circumstances has 1,3ee0 made to the firm, and the name of the owner of the Upg's submitted, and they now have the matter under consideration.

div.head: WARRINGTON 'CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.
div.p: WARRINGTON 'CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.
ANNUAL MEETING.

On Monday the annual meeting of the Chamber of Commerce was held in Bewsey Chambers. The vice-President (Councillor W. Pierpoint) presided, ,and there were also present Councillor J. H. Flem- tug, Mr. W. Long, Mr. J. Fairclough, Mr. W. Owen, Mr. J. L. Tunstall (hon. sec.), and Mr. C. Leigh (collector).

ARRlTrevrircoo tsi T.II DACIA nterrniss, &c. A.rePort of the Connoil signed by Mr. P. Stubs, the rrestdent, was submitted to the meeting:—" The Pre- sident attended, on behalf of the Chamber, the annual. Meeting of the Association of Chambers of Commerce. The Officials of the Government evinced a lively interest in the business of the meeting, Sir Michael Hicks Beach, President of the Board of Trade, having personally at- leaded. The resolution No. 9, re Boards of Arbitra- tion in labour disputes was passed unanimously. This recommends the establishment of Boards of conciliation 4nd arbitration by the various Chambers. The resolu- tion No. 23, re the scheme of Commercial Education Of the London Chamber, and urging each member to tremise preference to those holding a commercial cer- Qficate, and also to promote the institution of special echolaltships for efficiency in special subjects was unani- rnously passed, Sir John Lubbock having spoken very Well in support. With reference to the question of Boards of Arbitration in labour disputes, it will be within the .reeollection of some of the members of the Chamber, that a body was formed by the Warrington Chamber atay years ago. Its services have, however,never been into requisition. The scheme of Commercial education the London chamber, has now been put into operation t71.(1 many of the best commercial houses have pledged ,yetnsetves to give the preference to applicants for em- g,hyment holding the commercial certificates. The Coun- torvrarded a copy of the syllabus to the Warrington hers' Association, but the latter have as yet taken • action in the matter. The Council,. acting in concert L,.411 the Corporation of Warrrington,and other interested thorities, recently approached the Manchester Ship Vial Company, with a view to inducing them to build ijaProposed bridge over the Mersey at Walton, at a ,Tsher level than that shown on the plans, as otherwise, to the low headway, communication with the from the river would have been cut off for boats tit• even very Moderate size. There is every prospect of O bridge in question being built on the same levelrkthe London and North-Western railway Bridges, in I,...tich case the headway will be ample. Arrangements • been made with the Admiralty for the exhibition • the Chamber next-spring, of samples of such heavy fu'Lher goods as they may require, so as to give greater acility to persons desiring to teuder for their supply." f FLEMING moved the adoption of the report. Re- og to the arrangements that had been made for the /chibition of heavy leather goods, he said he hoped the Zadeset the town would reap some benefit from it.— hai Lox° said the report showed that the Chamber , done good work in the past year. With regard to ;, facilities for a bridge over the Ship Canal works, he Iffe_einned that had come about very much by the action • t4le Chamber, and it had been promptly' taken up by Te Town Council.—Mr. ToNsraze said the thing was srst suggested by Mr. Fairclough.—The CHAIRMAN :As Member of this Chamber.—Mr. LONG said with regard Zo education the action of the Chamber did not seem to aye been responded to by the educational authorities s.,7,the town.—Mr. TUNSTALL : It has not.— Mr. Lowo : ~70 have, I think, done all we can in that way.—Mr. !UNSTALL : We might approach them again.—Mr. FAlR- 'torGrr pointed out that the report said that a body Z'as formed by that Chamber some years ago to settle b.hour disputes. He should like to know if that body wae in working order. It ought he thought to be re- eretituted every year. -KEATING'S COUGH LOZENGES. "94, Commercial Road, Peckham, July 12, 1889. 'Dear Sir,—l am a poor hand at expressing my feelings on paper, but I should like to thank you, for your lozenges have done wonders tor me in relieving my terrible cough. Since I had the operation of Tracheetomy ' (the same as the late Emperor of Germany, and unlike him, thank God, I am still aliveend getting on well) performed at St. Bartholomew's Hospital for abduct, or paralysis of the vocal chords, no one could possibly have had a more violeint cough • indeed, it was so bad at times that it quite ex,riisted me. The mucus also, which was very copious and hard, has been softened, and I , have been able to get rid of it without difficalty.—l am, sir, yours truly, "Mr. T. Keating."

THE KNOWLES-DUNCAN APPEAL.

On Thursday the application of the defendant in the Knowles-Duncan breach of promise case for a new trial, on the ground of excessive damages, came before the Appeal Court. The Solicitor-General appeared for Leslie Fraser Duncan, the defendant, and Mr. Willis for Miss Gladys Knowles. The Solicitor-General read the corres- pondence, and reviewed the evidence in the case. Mr. Willis submitted that defendant never intended to marry plaintiff, and that his proposals were made with a view to seduce her. After further hearing the case was adjourned. Yesterday Mr. Willis concluded his argu- ments for the plaintiff. The Solicitor!General added that the defendant's property had been realized, and amounted to £8,500. The Master of the Rolls then an- nounced that the court would reduce the damages to £6,500. with taxed costs of trial and appall. If the plaintiff refused that she could have a 'new trial. The plaintiff's counsel accepted the reduced damages and costa. ROYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS A.U. (WARRINGTON DISTRICT) AND CHILDREN'S
SCHOOL FEES.

Sir,—l see from the newspapers that a discussion took place at a meeting held by the Warrington Board of Guardians. on Wednesday last, on the report of Mr. Basil Shearer, inquiry officer, who stated that it had occurred to him that it would be useful to compare the number of applications for school fees for several meetings during the recent hard weather with the same number during the same period in past years. lam very pleased to in- form your readers that the above district step in and pay the school fees of all deceased members' children, so that the widow may not have to appeal to the Board of Guardians for relief in that form. The above district at the present time is paving through the District Treasurer, Mr. John Allen, school fees at the Parochial Schools, Heath Side School, People's College, St. Mary's School, Buttermarket-st., Holy Trinity School, Christ Church School, (Latchford), Hamilton-st. School—in fact almost all the public schools in Warrington. The fund is being raised by a voluntary levy of the members each quarter with the addition of a few donations from gentlemen of the town. But for this excellent fund Mr. Shearer might have had a large num- ber of applications for school fees to report.—l am, sir, yours truly, ABEL HENRY MATHER, District Secretary. [P.S.—This fund was established April sth, 1879, and is now paying school fees for over twenty children.]

div.head: SALARIES OF RUNCORN OFFICIALS.
div.p: SALARIES OF RUNCORN OFFICIALS.

Sir,—With much pleasure, I read the able letter of your anonymous Correspondent " Qui Vive " which appeared in your valuable journal of last Saturday touching the present enormous and ever increasing salaries paid to the officers of the. ratepayers of this poverty-stricken little town. Much has already been said and written on this subject from time to time by the poor suffering ratepayers, but evidently all to no purpose. A stranger living at a distance would naturally ask—why elect representatives whose little minds are not capable of seeing, far lest repelling, the fulsome flattery and adulations of any officer seeking promotion beyond a fair and reasonable wage? lam afraid, sir, such an one has never witnessed an election here. The secret of being elected here is to employ on the day of election half-a-dozen or more low, stalwart loafers well filled with booze, to capture and carry the poor benighted voters, like sheep to the slaughter. to the polling booth, make them sign their name to a paper already filled up, and deposit it with the returning officer befare they are allowed to regain their liberty. Such is the state of matters here, to cope with which, I believe it is rumoured in the town as a last resource to call in the assistance of Captain Boycott, or as Gladstone very properly designates the operations of this illustrious individual whose brilliant services have proved so beneficial elsewhere," Exclusive dealing." Give them a taste of this, and be they shopkeepers,manufacturers, or anything else, we will soon see them dealing with the ratepayers' hard-earned money in a different fashion. I guess there will be no highly-paid men doing little or anything from one week's end to another but burning the ratepayers' coal and gas.—Yours truly, RATEPAYER. Runcorn, January 28th, 1891.

div.head: INSPIRATION AD REVELATION.
div.p: INSPIRATION AD REVELATION.

Sir,—Mr. Peers speaks of confusion in the very title of my last letter. That title, sir, was prefixed by yourself, and I must ask you kindly to accept the responsibility for it, though I myself find no fault with it. It was your injunction to Mr.. Peers and others to be brief which led me to say what I had to say in as few words as possible, and therefore to embody my mean- ing in metaphor ; and although I am charged with being vague, general, and confused, yet it is plain that Mr. Peers understood me, and that in gaining brevity I did not altogether lose lucidity.

Mr. Peers must forgive me if I again occasionally clothe my meaning in a figure of speech. The subject under discussion embraces so vast a territory of thought that a minute exanination of its surface within the compass of a letter to a newspaper is impossible. Something in the nature of a bird's-eye view is all that can be attempted. I tried to show in my last letter that Mr. Peers's rejec- tors and believers are at one in regarding the Bible as an

-- entity, a homogeneous whole. To both each particle of its substance is like every other particle with regard to divine inspiration. They only differ (i.e. the Rejectors and Believers) as to the presence or absence of such inspiration in each and every part. Both demand the right to take any portion of the book at random and exhibit it as a sample of the whole—much as a factor samples a cheese and purchases or not accordingly. Now, it seems to me that the Bible is an entity only in a sense that as a book it is contained within two covers. In the purport and intrinsic value of its c ontents it is by no means so. To me—and 1 am sure to the majority of Christians—a proeof filtration, or precipitation,rather than of sampling is what the Bible requires, and in some parts, (to change the figure somewhat) something in the nature of a dredging operation, that shall plunge deep down beneath the superincambent mass of obstructive matter and bring truth to the surface. Mr. Peers will see that Iregard the Bible with eyes very different from those of either his Rejector or ,Believer. The mere fact of so many ancient documents coming to- gether between the same covers is not a sufficientground

for any claim of homogeneity of substance. And there- fore I am not bound to either accept or reject the whole on account of any single part. To do so would lot to hold a cast-iron theory of inspiration which is unwarranted by any claims made by the book itself. Mr. Peers asks a question about the validity of con- clusions if drawn from wrong premises, instancing' the definitions and propositions of "my beloved" Euclid. Now, in the implied conclusion Mr. Peers begs the whole question as far as the Bible is concerned. Euclid treats exclusively of Geometry ; his definitions, axioms, and the like are the indispensable foundations of his superstruc- ture, and, if one may so speak, structure and super- • structure are composed of the same material. But would Mr. Peers have us believe that the physical science of the Bible is the foundation and of the essence of the Bible in the sense that Euclid's definitions are the founda- tion and of the essence of his Geometry? Is the Bible a book dealing exclusively with science? Do the ethical precepts of its prophets and lawgivers and of Christ de- pend for their stability on the physical statements of the Bible? And because;the cosmogony of Genesis is not satisfactory, are the ten Commandments therefore invalid ? We may go even further. right conclusion is not always drawn from correct premises, and it would be possible to extract truth from Euclid even though some of his definitions halted.. As a matter of fact, Mill comments very severely on Euclid's definitions of point and a line. Ido not say Mill is right. I believe he is wrong. What I wish to point out is that Mill never dreamt of rejecting the whole of Euclid's system because of thesupposed flaws in his premises. And when it is remembered that the physical science of the Bible is not the essence of the Bible, that is is not even a portion of its foundation, it will be seen how utterly unwarrant- able is a rejection of the whole book for reasons so feeble. Now the Bible is not a revelation : it is the record of a revelation; and that revelation is not of physical truth but of God.—His nature and, character, and His rela- tion to man. Mr. Peers is an evolutionist; he holds the development of nature and of the knowledge of nature. Indeed no one can believe anything else about know- ledge—(and yet he expects to find in a very ancient document a knowledge of nature which it has taken man ages to acquire). Apply this reasoning to the knowledge of God as seen in the recorded Revelation in the Bible (for what is growing knowledge in its human aspect is growing revelation in its divine). Such know- ledge proceeds from less to greater; the glimmer of the dawn becomes the full light of day. "He that hath seen me," says Christ," bath seen the Father." Mr. Peers must surely grant that, assumiug th 3 existence of God and that He was the Creator of that life which ulti- mately appeared upon the earth in the " jelly-speck "of science, that first protoplasmic atom which eventuated in man—he must grant, I say, that sonfe such process of enlightenment and apprehension of his relation to his Creator as we find recorded in the Bible must have been experienced by man. If the revelation of God with ' which the Bible is supremely and essentially- concerned, culminated, as I believe, in Christ's advent, it is.e easy to see howl arrive at my conclusion about the central point of the biblical system. And therefore it cannot matter a pin's point where the geometrical centre of the Bible as a book may be; the question is which is its substan- tial, essential centre, its centre of gravity. And so, regarding Christ as a perfect presentation and revelation of God, the knowledge of whom as held by the antece- dent prophets and seers was so intermixed with error, I hold that He is able to enlighten that moral sense to which He himself appeals and must submit Himself as that moral truth' which is but an aspect of the character of God, may be followed into its most hidden ramifica- tions, and that the whole may be welded into a perfect and harmonious system. I know what Mr. Peers will say :—" You assume three things :-1. The existence of God; 2. That Christ " claimed to be the supreme revelation of God of which you speak; 3. The validity of such claims if made. To such objections I may possibly reply when Mr. Peers has dealt with my main argument in this letter. Yours &c., MASTER OF ARTS.

THE SCOTCH RAILWAY STRIKE. A STATION BURNT DOWN. The Calderbank station of the Caledonian Railway Company was destroyed by fire on Monday morning, as the result,it is believed, of incendiarism. The remains of a barrel of paraffin oil were found in the ladies' waiting- room, the barrel having been removed from the store- house, and there were marks of a forcible entry in the signal cabin and store telow. The books, papers, and cash were saved in the office safe.

At a mass meeting on Tuesday the men resolved to continue the strike. On Tuesday a petition was pre- sented to the Court of Session, on 'behalf of Mr. Tate, to recall the arrestments issued by the North British Rail- way Company against the bfficials of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants of Scotland. It is alleged that certain moneys have been arrested which do not belong to the society. At Glasgow Messrs. Tait and Burns were on Tuesday as confident as ever respeJting the position of the Scotch railway strikers. They received a telegram from Carlisle stating that -Mr_ Thompson, the Caletionian_general manager, wished to meet the men ar 40-On, but sthelatter refused to attend. The Gasgow Caledonian authorities report that a number of masked men maltreated engine cleaners working at Strathaven sheds, and threw an engine hito the turntable pit. The local officials of the Caledonian Company have received a telegram from Mr. Thompson, the general manager, intimating that the directors have in conse- quence of the lawless conduct of the strikers at Perth, decided not to re-engage any of them, so that so far as titiat line is concerned the strike is now converted into a lock-out.

Speaking at Millwall,• London, on Tuesday evening, Mr. Asquith, M.P., condemned the insensate caprice and folly of the directors of the North British Railway in pro- longing the strike. The directors had said they were willing to go into the merits of the case, but there were no merits to be gone into. It was a case—if ever there was a case in the history of industrial warfare—where there was on one side a body ef men promulgating a claim which every impartial person admitted to be justi- fied, not only for reasons of expedience, but by every principle of elementary justice; and on the other side a small body of employers, who resisted that claim, not because it was no just, but because it was not put for- ward with what they considered to be the proper formalities:,

The Caledonian Railway officials at Glasgow on Wed- nesday reported that six men had been arrested At Hamilton in connection with Tuesday's outrage at Stra- Maven. The strikers received £50.5.. The strikers at Greenock are more confident; they are maintaining their ground ; but at Perth they are said to be going back to work. _

The North British officials stated on Wednesday that a number Of signalmen had resumed work, and the Cale- donian officials declare that there is no lack of men. In consequence of aspersions cast upon reporters by Mr. John Burns, the Scotch papers have resolved to cease reporting the men's meetings. SETTLEMENT ON THE NORTH BRITISH. The strike on the Scotch railways, which has lasted within a day or two of six weeks, has come to an end so far as one of the companies—the North British—is con- cerned. In the case of the Caledonian it was reported at a meeting of the men on Thursday night that Mr. Thom- son, the general manager, had declined to give the assurances which were obtained from the North British Company, and therefore the struggle in his case would be maintained. The officials of the Caledonian Company, however, state that their posi- tion now is such that they view the continuance of the strike with little concern. The men's leaders last night admitted that in the arrangement they had been able to make there was no provisions for a ten hours day or a sixty hours' week, but public attention had been so thoroughly called to the evils of overwork on railways that lonz stretches of duty would, on the Scotch systems at any rate, be in the future unknown; It would seem that the terms of settlement are, with the condition of the withdrawal by the Company of the action against the Railway Servants' Society, substanti- ally those offered by the Company at an earlier stage of the dispute. The men are to go in again, after which the employers will be prepared to consider any alleged grievances that they may wish to lay before them, and to coffer remedies where possible.
The North British Railway men were taken back at Glasgow on the terms arranged on Thursday. Those who did not find employment will be supported by the Strike Fund until vacancies arise.
The Caledonian men at Greenock, Carlisle, and Dun- dee, resolved yesterday to stay out.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JANUARY 31, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JANUARY 31, 1891.
EARL OF CARNARVON.
The Earl of Carnarvon was born on 24th of June, 831, and died on the 28th of June, 1890. During

[g his seat in the House of Lords, he made his maiden speech, on which he was highly complimented by Lord Derby, who, in 1859, nomin- ated him High Steward of the University of Oxford. He was Under-secretary of State for the Colonies in Lord Derby's second administration; 1858-9, and was appointed Secretary of State for the Colonies. in Lord Derby's third administration, June, 1866. On February 19th, 1867, he moved in the House of Lords the second reading of the Bill for the Con- federation of the British North American Provinces, which he truly described as one of the largest and most ipporrant measures that for many years it had been the duty of any Colonial Minister in this country to submit to Parliament. On March 2nd of the same year he • resigned the Colonial Secretary- ship on account of a difference of opinion respect- ing Parliamentary Reform. At the same time, General Peel was Secretary, and Lord Cranborne (now the Marquis of Salisbury) Secretary for India, tendered their resignations, which were accepted. On the formation of Mr. Disraeli's cabinet in Feb- urary, 1874, he was for the second time appointed Secretary of State for the Colonies. He resigned his seat in the Cabinet, January 24, 1878,in consequence of his disagreement with his colleagues as to the policy of ordering the British fleet to proceed to the Dardanelles. His lordship considered this to he a departure from the policy of neutrality which the Government had pledged themselves to preserve as long as neither of the belligerents infringed certain conditions which Her Majesty's Government itself had laid down. Lord Derby, Foreign Secretary, tendered his resignation at the same time, but con- sented to resume his post after the order respect- ing the fleet had been countermanded, and explan- ations had been made with his colleagues. During the short-lived administration of Lord Salisbury, in 1885, Lord Carnarvon held the office of Lord Lieutenant of Ireland. Among the publications of which Lord Carnarvon was author are "The Arch- wology of Berkshire " ; " Recollections of the Drus- es of the Lebanon; and notes on their religion " ; and a translation of the "Agamemnon " of Aeschy- lus. It was written of Lord Carnarvon, after his death, that "he studied men as well as books, and his range was singularly wide and varied. He was probably the only cabinet minister who could say that he had visited all the great colonies of the Empire. He was a greater wanderer than his hero Ulysses. Nor were his journeys confined to the British Enspire. From modern Paris to the ruins of Nineveh and Babylon there was hardly any ob- ject of interest which he had not visited and 'exam- ined with intelligence and care. The prejudices of culture and science, as powerful as those of bigotry and ignorance, never circumscribed the range of his sympathies."

div.p: LYMM.

THE POPULAR CONCERTS.—The weekly concert took place in the Bridgewater Rooms, on Saturday evening, when there was again a crowded attendance, about 180 being present. Mr. J. Mort occupied the chair, and Mr. Manning, Thelwall, gave an address. Song, Etc., were given by Mr. J. Thomason, Mr. J. H. Peters, Mr. Hall, Mr. Richard Dutton, Miss Marion Thorpe, the Chairman and Mr. George Smith. The accompaniments to the songs were played by Mr. Ted Smith and Miss Marion Thorpe.

MEETING 'AT THE CONSERVATIVE CUM—The annual meeting in connection with the Lymm Conservative and Constitutional Association washeld at the Club premises, Lymm Bridge, on Monday evening. Mr. Norris presided. Amongst those present were Messrs, A. W. Callender (secretary), T. Ardern (treasurer), H. Tetlow, F. Swallow, J. P. Newton (Warburton), Edward Gibbon, E. Massey, H. Harrison, J. Best, Richardson, &c. The new club, which is now externally completed, the secre- tary reported, would probably be opened toward mid- summer. The treasurer presented his accounts, and reported a balance of about £5 on the year's working. The election of officers for the ensuing year was then proceeded with, the following being selected :--Presi- dent, Colonel Fl. Cornwall Legh ; vice-presidents, Messrs. Peter Stubs, J.P., T. P. Norris, J.P., and William Battersby ; Committee: Messrs. Groves Edwards Massey, H. Tetlow, J. R. Newton, H. Groves, F. Swallow, Harrison, Woodhead, E. Gibbon, T. P. Norris, P. Stubs, W. Battersby and Martin. Messrs. Norris, Stubs, Callender, and Tetlow were appointed delegates to the Central Consultative Committee at Altrincham.-

div.head: SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL
THELWALL

The genial spring-like weather of the past few days has been welcomed by all directly interested in the Ship Canal. For over six weeks King Frost has reigned supreme, and the work almost along the line, and par- ticularly along the Latchford and Thelwall sections, has been greatly delayed. The weather has afforded little opportunity of rectifying the damage occasioned by the recent flood, and a quantity of wreckage is still strewn about the bottom of the cutting. Preparations are being made for repairing the railways which were totally dis- arranged. The Latchford locks are incomplete, and the gigantic bridge by which the railway will cross the entire width of the canal is but partially constructed. Brickwork on either side of the cutting is practically finished, but the iron work has not yet been commenced. Operations connected with the other incomplete bridges at Wash-lane, an the one over the Knutsford-road near the railway, are to be resumed. The road extending th. Dog ama_ttaxtlnn, Grappenhall, over the rail- way has been been very much raised. It was intend that the roads should be lowered and go under the new me, but this plan was found difficult to carry out.

div.head: RIXTON.
div.p: RIXTON.

No. 6 cutting of the Latchford Section was in an advanced state of completion when the heavy floods which occurred last year took place. The water, it will be remembered, broke through into the cutting, taking with it the dredger moored near. This dredger after having broken the bridge across the Canal, was over- turned by the collision, and portions of it can now be seen protruding above the water. From the time when this misfortune happened, until last week, nothing has been done except to stop the gap, to alter the route, and to mend the temporary bridge. At the present time two powerful centrifugal pumps, besides the stationary beam pumps, are at' work, and if nothing happens the water will soon be cleared out. However, on Saturday morn- ing, the cutting was in imminent danger of again filling, owing to the sadden thaw. It was only through the energy of the agent that this misfortune was averted. This cutting cuts Newbridge-lane, and it was at first proposed to place A swing bridge across the Canal at this point. This scheme is now rejected, and a suspension bridge is to be placed some fifty yards from the original point. Excavations for the basement of the buttresses are now rapidly proceeding, together with " tipping " for the approaches.

div.head: BORROWING. POWERS
div.p: BORROWING. POWERS

At a special meeting of the shareholders of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company, held in the Concert Hall, on Thursday under the presidency of the Chairman of the Company, Lord Egerton of Tatton, the Directors were given authority to borrow the sum of £453,000. Under the Ship Canal Acts of 1885 and 1886 powers were given to borrow £1,812,000. • Of that sum £1,359,000 had already been issued, and the sum which the Direc- tors received authority on Thursday to raise represents the balance hitherto unissued.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

PARISH CHURCIL—TV/0 sermons were preached in the Parish Church, Frodsham, on Sunday, on behalf of the Curates' Augmentation Fund, by the Rev. E. O.Rawson, vicar of Ince. The offertories for the day amounted to £lO 4s. 4d. UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES.—The second lecture on" Victorian writers" was delivered in the Town Hall Frodsham. on Wednesday- evening, by Mr. E. H. Spen, der, 8.A., "Tennyson " being the subject of the lecture. There was a good attendance. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—At a meeting of this class, last night week, Mr. Robert Holland delivered a lecture on the history and customs of Cheshire, which was full of interesting and instructive information as to the notable sayings and doings of the men in Cheshire. At the close the vote of thanks was proposed by Mr. Williams, seconded by Mr. R. Proud. CONSERVATIVE CLUB BUILDING CO.. LIMITED.—A com- pany has been lately formed under the Joint Stock Com- panies Acts, 1882 to 1890, for the purpose of erecting a building suitable for a Conservative Club for Frodsham. the premises situate in Church-st. at present occupied being unsuitable. The capital iS £2,000, divided into 2,000 shares of £1 each, and of which it is proposed at present to issue one half. A piece of land in Main-st., Frodsham,ha.s been given by the Marquis of Cholmonde- ley for a term of 999 years, at a nominal rent, so long as the building to be erected shall be used for a Conserva- tive Club. Lima's° DISTRICT.—A meeting of the ratepayers within the Frodsham Lighting Distriot, was held in the Overseers' Office., Frodslia m , on Wednesday.evening,when Mr. Thomas Davies, senior overseer of the Frodsham township, presided. The accounts of the Gas Inspector for the past year were produced by the secretary (Mr. Samuel Davies), and adopted. The following gentlemen were then nominated as inspectors for the same period: —Dr. Weaver, Messrs. Robert Holland, H. G. Linaker, William ,Booth (farmer), John Austin, James Illidge, and Alex. Bate. After some discussion relative to the poor lighting of the district, it was resolved that the Gas Company be asked to reduce the price of. gas, and to provide a better quality:. A vote of thanks to the Chair- man concluded the business.
Mr. Justice-Senne, the newly appointed Judge,took his seat in the Probate Division on Thursday. SERVANTS' BALL AT NEWTON.

On Tuesday evening the annual ball given by Col. McCorquodale to his servants, took place in the Town Hall, Newton. The room had been nicely decorated for the occasion, and including the ser- vants and invited guests, there were about 80 per- sons present. Dancing was spiritedly indulged in until about five o'clock on Wednesday morning, to .music supplied by Mr. Peplow's string band. The arrangements,which were of an excellent character, were in the hands of Mr. Haynes, butler. During the intervals songs, &c., were given by various members of the company, and the health of Col. McCorquodale and family was drunk on the proposi- tion of Mr. Haynes.
CANON LIDDON.

of England suffered the loss of one of ‘aments when Canon Liddon breathed his last on the 9th of September last. Writing soon after that, melancholy event in the "Now Review " A.rchdeacon Pott said of lanon Liddon, " As a preacher is influence, has been unique our time—more powerful, I believe, even thantthat of le present bishop of Peter-

bishop of Wilberforce, notwith- standing the close logic of the former and the per- suasive rhetoric of the latter; for Liddon combined the two. Profound and ever-increasing stores of learning, careful study and prepargion, great power of language, a clear distinct intonation, and withal that great force which earnest personal con- viction brings with it, these seem to me to have been some of the elements of his strength. It has been said that his style was formed upon French rather than English models. True, so far, that be held the great French preachers to have reached the highest perfection of pulpit oratory. Bourdalone was his ideal ; but Liddon was no copyist either in matter or manner." This great preacher was born in 1829. He became a student of Christ Church, Oxford, where he graduated B.A. in 1850, taking a second class in Classics. In 1851 he obtained the Johnson Theological Scholarship, and in 1853, he proceeded to the degree of M.A. Having taken orders, he was, from 1854 to 1859, vice,Principal of the Theological ColJege of Caddesdon. He was also examining chaplain to the late Bishop of Salisbury. In 1864 he was appointed prebendary of Major Pars Altaris in Salisbury Cathedral. In 1870 he was installed' a Canon residentiary of St. Paul's Cathedral, and in the same year be was ap- pointed Irelana professor of the Exegesis of the Holy Scripture in the Uhiversity of Oxford. Canon Liddon was the author of several theological publi- cations.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. BRADLAUGH.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. BRADLAUGH.

The following bulletin was issued yesterday morn- ing—" Mr. Bradlaugh died from uremia at 6:30 a.m. quietly and peacefully." The Central News says: —lt was hoped as late as Thursday morning that Mr.' Bradlaugh's constitution would enable him to fight successfully through the severe illness from which he suffered, but on Thursday afternoon a change for the worse set in, his strength gradually ebbed away, and in the early hours of yesterday morning it wAs seen that he was completely exhaus- ted. He passed away quietly at 6-30 o'clock, his daughter, Mrs. Bonner, being with him. Mr. Brad- laugh, who had been in feeble health for some months past, was attacked a few weeks ago with cardiac asthma of so serious a type that it was feared from the first that he would not get over it. His illness, though for some time serious, did not take an alarming turn until "a week ago, when he had passed a night of pain and sleeplessness. He recov- ered somewhat during the day, and dictated two letters, but, in the evening he grew worse, and Dr. Bell was summoned. He found that a blood vessel had given way in the head, causing grave complications in the patient's condition. Next morning Dr. Bristowe, Mr. Bradlaugh's colleague on the Vaccination Commission, was summoned and made care- ful and complete examinations of the patient. He said there was a bare chance that the ruptured blood-vessel might heal ; and that appeared to take place during Saturday and Sunday, and on Monday Dr. Kamskill and Dr. Bell reported favourably on Mr. Bradlaugh's case. On Tuesday, however, his condition was again worse, and the heart's action became feebler.

The news was received at Northampton with general expressions of regret, and on receipt of Mrs. Bradlaugh Bonner's telegram announcing the sad event, numerous messages of c9ndolence were despatched by individuals of all classes.

It was the principal topic of conversation at all the London political clubs yesterday morning, and the regret which was expressed was intensified by the belief that Mr. Bradlaugh never sufficiently recovered consciousness to receive the news that the House of Commons ex- punged the resolution of 1380. Mr. Bradlaugh, who was 53 years of age, will be buried on the "earth-to-earth" principle, at Brookwood (Surrey) Cemetery, on Tuesday.' There will be no dis- play or procession in London, and the coffin will be privately removed from St. John's Wood. Friends who may attend the burial are requested not, to -.rem. mourn- ing. The interment will take place in the usual manner, but there will be no funeral service.

Mr. Charles Bradlaugh was the son of the late Charles Bradlaugh, by Mary, daughter of James Trimby. He was born at Hoxton' London, in 1833, and married in 1854 Susannah Lamb, daughter of Mr. Abraham Hooper, of Middlehurst, Sussex. His wife died in 1877. He was well known as a lecturer and as editor and proprietor of the "National Reformer." He was also president of the National Secular Society. In politics he was an advanced Radical, and a staunch supporter of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule policy. He was also strongly in favour of the abolition of primogeniture, Disestablishment, &c. He was first returned for Northampton in April, 'lBBO, and on its being decided by a court of law that he was not a person to affirm, instead of subscribing to the oath he again stood for election and was returned a second tiine in April, 1881. On being ex- pelled the House of Commons he was re-elected in March, 1882, and on February 11th,1884. he toted in the House. He was again excluded by resolution, and then applied for the Chiltern Hundreds. For a fourth time Northampton elected him, but owing to the contrary decision of the law courts he did not take his seat till the dissolution. At the general elections of 1885 and 1886 lie was again elected, and has shared the represent- ation of the borough in conjunction with Mr. Labouchere ever since. Since his early encounters he has advanced rapidly in public and Parliamentary esteem, and only on Tuesday last the House of Commons unanimously agreed to expunge from the records of the House the resolution by which he was years ago excluded.

SPECIAL SERMON.

On Thursday evening the pulpit of the Wesleyan Chapel was occupied by the Rev. Thomas Champ- ness, of Rochdale. A powerful sermon was preached from the second book of Kings, sth chapter. The sermon was attentively listened to by a large con- gregation. A collection was taken at the close of the service on behalf of the chapel extension. MUTUAL IMPROVEAIRNT ASSOCIATION.

On Wednesday evening in connection with the above association a miscellaneous entertainment was given by the membls, Ur. D. Garnett in the chair. Short papers were contributed by several of the members, a song by Mr. D. Garnett,and a piano- forte solo by Miss Mabel Garnett. A most enjoy- able evening was spent. LIBERAL TEA.-PARTY AND CONCERT.

Last evening week the annual tea-party and con- cert in connection with the Penketh Liberal Asso- ciation was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom. About 120 persons sat down to an excellent knife and fork tea consisting of beef, ham, salmon, sweet- meats, &c. It was prepared by Mesdames Mainley, Routledge, Longshaw, White, Marsland,and Wilkin- son. The following ladies presided at the tables: Misses Seed, Hughes, Griffiths, Al ainley, Cross. and L. Routledge. After tea the room was arranged for the concert. A most excellent programme was pro- vided. Owing to the unavoidable absence, through illness, of Mr. J. T. Gumersall, the chair was occu- pied by Mr. R. Garnett. The programme consisted of songs, recitations, &c., contributed by various friends in a manner which was greatly appreciated by the audience. At the conclusion of the pro- gramme the room was cleared and a variety of games were indulged in till 11 o'clock.

EARLESTOWN GOOD TEDIPLARS.

The usual weekly Session was held on Monday evening last in the Lodge-room, Bridge-st., when Bro. J. F. Singleton, C.T. presided over, a very good attendance of members. After the opening, four candidates were admitted to membership in the lodge. Bro. John Taylor, L.D., read circulars from the D. Sec. relative to a projected tepperance de- monstration under the auspices of the district lodge. It was resolved to arrange for paying a visit to the "Hope of Wigan" lodge. Bros. George Clarke, George B. Warburton jun., with Bro. John Taylor L.D. were elected representatives to the South-west Lancashire District Lodge, for the ensuing 12 months. Brothers John Taylor L.D., George Clarke, George E. Warburton, and A. Morris were elecOd regular representatives, and Sister E. Clarke, Sister J. E. Warburton, and Bro. W. Shaw, alternate repre- sentatives to the monthly sessions of No. 1 Con- vention for the ensuing half-year. Several other iteras.were transacted,after which Bro. J. F. Single- ton C.T. concluded his paper on "The History of Good Templary," for which he received the thanks of the lodge. A number of melodies, songs, &c., , were rendered by various members, a very pleasant and encouraging Session concluding to usual.

div.head: CHURCH OF THE FUTURE.
div.p: THE CHURCH OF THE FUTURE.

• On Sunday morning at Cairo-st ,Chapel, warring-* ton, the Rev. Frank K. Freeston discoursed on the above subject. After defining the church as an institution for the expression, cultivation, and pro- ' motion of religion, and then pointed out where the church of to-day fails to fulfil its high condition, he thus summarried a few of the features which he thought would marl- the Church of the Future. 1. It will have no limitations. Though still divided on non-essentials,it will be united en the broad and unfenced ground of common humanity. Its motto and its method will be "In things essential unity, in things doubtfal liberty, in all things charity." 2:. It will place life and deed before belief and creed. Instead of insisting on " tangled trinities," and instead of pronouncing who is a Christian, who not, it will be content and ready to say "Christian 19 that Christian does," Fear God and keep His com- mandments, for. this is the whole duty of man."' 3, It will pioneer, instead of follow after, all good work.. It will do good for good's own sake, and not cripple. or confine its work by raising theological testa 4 it will therefore preach self-sacrifice. Raised aloft as the ideal for all will be thespirit and practice of self-sacrifice. That will be accepted fla' the proof of real religion, that will be demanded na the duty of the church. 5.. It will offer ampler choice of Christian service. Laymen of everydegree, women, and even children, will be called to take their part in the church's work, and no church will be touching its ideal until every single member is engaged in personal service. It will be the 3foral University of the world, the universal school of virtue in which are taught to all alike the duties of a righteous and godly life. 7. It will co-operate .with all its parts for the united and extended per- formance of strictly unsectarian service, meetin national needs with national effort and local wants with local alliance. 8. It will Jra.w together the church and the world, no longer holding.aloof in selfish and too libly seclusion, but combining the service of God with. the service of MIMI and so bring- ' .ing nearer the time when the. kingdoms of the world shall have become the kingdoms of our Lord and.of His Christ.

pUNCORN UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTIIO- - RITY.—THE PUBLICHEALTH ACT, 1875. FROD- SHAM WATER SUPPLY. The Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary Authority being the Local Authority under the Public Health Act, 1875, for the district of Frodsham Township, in the County of Chester, hereby give notice pursuant to Station 53 of the said Act, that they intend, at the expiration of not less than two months from the publication hereof, to commence the con- struction of a Reservoir to hold one hundred and twenty-five thousand gallons at water, or thereabouts, and do such other works in connection therewith as may be necessary for pro- viding a supply of water to the said Township of Frodsham. It is proposed to sink a well on land belonging to John Hig- son, Esq., in Frodsham Marsh. and pump the water therefrom to the said reservoir to be built on land belonging to the Re- presentatives of the late Mrs. Perryn. in Overton, in the Township of Frodsham Lordship, and that any person who would be affected by the intended work, objecting to such work. Is required within the said two months to serve notice in writing of such objection, on the said Authority, by send- ing such notice through the post, addressed to the Authority, or to me, or by delivering the same to me in person. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that an Extraordinary General MEETING of this Company will be held at the Bank Premises, Winwick-street, Warrington. on Friday, the 13th day of February, 1891. at Twelve o'clock, for the purpose of considering, and, if thought expedient, confirming the Special Resolution hereto appended, which was passed at an Extra- ordinary General meeting, held on the 23rd January, 1891, viz. : " That the Articles of Association of the Company be altered by the Insertion therein of the following Article, namely : No. 114 A.—The dividend, extraordinary dividend, or bonus payable upon shares in respect of which any person is, under the Company's Articles relating to the transfer and transmission of shares, entitled to become a member, or which any person under those Articles is entitled to transfer, shall, unless the Directors in their uncontrolled discretion othetwise appoint, be retained until such person shall become a member in respect of such shares, or shall duly transfer the same, and every transfer of such shares shall carry with it all dividends, extraordinary divi- dends, or I onuses which may have been retained as herein provided." By order, JOHN DUN, Old Bank, Warrington, General Manager. 26th January, 1891.
